Static analysis only; no game process was run.

categories.summary: Crank parts share one RPS state with inertia I = 1 + Σ engine_max_force. Each undamaged cylinder above 2 RPS adds 80000 × burned fuel × efficiency ÷ I RPS per update, fuel stops above 60 RPS, the mixture peaks at AFR 13.6 + 0.4t, and the crank keeps 1 - 0.01 × (1 - F ÷ I) of its speed each update.

sections.title: Crank group and inertia
sections.body: Crankshafts, converters, cylinders, drive belts, power manifolds and flywheels joined by crank, belt or cylinder couplings form one crank group with one RPS value. The group starts at inertia I = 1 and frictionless sum F = 0. Each member adds its engine_max_force to I and its engine_frictionless_force to F: crankshafts 0.7, 8, 15 and 25; converters 8 and 15; cylinders 0.6, 12 and 15; the drive belt 0.6; power manifolds 5; flywheels 150, 600 and 2400. Only flywheels have a nonzero F, equal to their inertia weight. Clutches, the starter, alternator and fluid pump add nothing to I. Converters and belts change no speed in their own update, so every member turns at the crank RPS, 1:1.

sections.title: Speed each update
sections.body: First the crank keeps r × (1 - 0.01 × (1 - F ÷ I)): 0.99 per update without a flywheel, 0.54716 after one simulated second of coasting. Then each cylinder in turn adds Δr = gain × burned fuel × efficiency ÷ I, with gain 80000 at damage 0, 40000 at damage 1 to 19 and no impulse from damage 20. Burned fuel is r × 0.000004 × voxels × fuel throttle when the crank is above 2 RPS and not above 60 RPS, the mixture is inside the window and the exhaust has room. With ideal supply one cylinder adds 0.32 × r × voxels × throttle × efficiency ÷ I per update. A later cylinder starts from the speed the earlier ones left, and the 60 RPS cut is tested before each impulse, so the crank can pass 60 within one update.

sections.title: Worked example
sections.body: At 20 °C, peak mixture and full throttle, starting at 20 RPS: one 1x1 cylinder on a 1x1 crankshaft (I = 2.3) ends the update at 22.1114 RPS, four 1x1 cylinders (I = 4.1) at 25.343 RPS, and the same four with a 1x1 flywheel (I = 154.1, F = 150) at 20.1339 RPS. The flywheel cuts both the coasting loss and each impulse.

sections.title: Combustion window
sections.body: Each cylinder computes a fuel term (RPS × 4e-6 × voxels × fuel throttle) and an intake term (RPS × 2.8e-6 × voxels ÷ 60 × air throttle × pressure factor). At 60 updates per simulated second the fuel term is RPS × 0.00024 × voxels × fuel throttle per second. The displayed air:fuel ratio is intake × 600 ÷ fuel, so with equal throttles and no boost it reads 7. Combustion happens only when the ratio lies between 12 − 2t and 16 + 4t, where t is the manifold temperature in °C ÷ 100 clamped to 0…1. Within the window the mixture factor 1 − 2(s − 0.6)² peaks at an air:fuel ratio of 13.6 + 0.4t: 13.68 at 20 °C and 14 at or above 100 °C. The fuel and air throttles are the largest inputs among the group's intake and air manifolds, taken once per group update; they are not summed.

sections.title: Heat, coolant and damage
sections.body: Burned fuel heats the shared manifold group by 6000 × burned fuel ÷ C, where C = 1 + 40 × the group's cylinder voxels; manifold extensions add nothing to C. Engine and coolant temperatures are in °C. Each group update the coolant moves k of the gap toward the engine and the engine loses W × k × gap ÷ C, with W the fresh plus sea water amount and k = 0.04 × (liquid amount ÷ total amount) × (1 - 0.8 × scaling)³. Clean water gives k = 0.04, fully scaled water 0.00032. Sea water above 100 °C builds scaling. Above 115 °C, with the engine_overheating and vehicle_damage settings both on, a cylinder takes 1 damage at once and 1 more every 300 updates, 5 simulated seconds, up to 50. Damage is the component's saved damage field. Shared spatial damage and repair routines also call the damage setter; repair lowers damage by an amount its caller passes, never below 0.

sections.title: Pressure and units
sections.body: Manifold and pipe pressures are in atmospheres, on the same law as the Tank Pressure output. The intake factor clamp(1 + 0.01 × mean air-manifold pressure, 1, 2) is 1.01 at 1 atm and reaches 2 at 100 atm. Crank and accessory speeds are RPS and temperatures °C. Inertia weights, heat in amount × °C and electrical charge are internal units.

limitations: All engine formulas are reconstructed from static decompilation of build f9206d85…; they were not checked in a running game.

For active, normally simulated vehicles, these formulas run once per nominal 1/60-second simulation update. Multiply per-update amounts by 60 for amounts per simulated second. A constant relaxation fraction k leaves (1-k)^60 of a gap after one simulated second. Physics solver substeps and render frames are separate; pauses, sleeping, unloaded vehicles and real-time slowdown are outside this conversion.
SI torque, power and energy were not recovered: the inertia weights, RPS impulses, heat in amount × °C and electrical charge have no established conversion to N m, watts or joules.

Modular registration and connection grouping are decoded, but the editor's complete placement and alignment validator was not traced. Which attachment positions and orientations the editor accepts is open beyond the coupling names the crank and manifold walks follow.

Beyond overheat, restore and the capped setter, shared spatial damage and repair routines call component damage setters, and repair subtracts a caller-supplied amount and clamps at 0. Collision attribution, damage thresholds, tool cadence and complete repair rates were not traced.

categories.summary: This catch-all holds sensors, radios, lights, fluid fittings, connectors, winches, doors and tools. Definitions give the ranges: v2 radios 100 m to 20 km with legacy radios configured identically, and radar ranges from 5000 to 500000 m. Radars and sonars pass a target when its physics-body mass over distance beats a fixed threshold, and the transponder locator pulses faster near a beacon. Radio signal strength falls linearly with distance over a reach set by both antennas' rx_range.

sections.title: Radio ranges
sections.body: rx_range equals the tooltip's ground-level range on every v2 radio (100, 1000, 4000, 20000) and on the directional antennas (8000000, 10000000). The legacy radios carry the same rx_range values as their v2 counterparts and run the same receive code. The tooltip figure is the distance at which two equal antennas fall to strength 0.5 (directional ones when exactly aligned); they still hear each other out to twice that.

sections.title: Radio signal strength
sections.body:
All radios, legacy, v2, video and directional, share one receive routine. A receiver hears a transmitter on the same frequency when the two pass a mode test, and keeps only the strongest signal; signals never add. Strength is S = (1 − d ÷ R) × g_r × g_t for antennas d metres apart in a straight line, and the signal is lost at d = R. Ordinary and video antennas have gain g = 1.

At full power with both antennas at sea level, R is the receiver's rx_range plus the transmitter's: 200 m for two Small, 20100 m for Small and Huge, 40000 m for two Huge. Each end's power fraction multiplies R, so half power at both ends gives 0.25 R. A height bonus H = 128000 × clamp(1 − (0.5 A(y_t) + A(y_r)))² m per end, with A(y) = (1 − 2.2413793e-05 × min(y, 40000))^5.3595023, adds range only when the receiver is high: above about 5413 m with the transmitter at sea level, or above about 3251 m with both at one altitude. A high transmitter alone adds nothing. Below y = 0 the range shrinks, to 0.25 R with both antennas submerged.

No terrain, obstacle, weather or random term takes part. After selection a level field in the received audio and video blocks is scaled by clamp(2 × S), full out to half of R (inference: their signal level). Composite data is copied unscaled, and the strength value itself is not scaled.

sections.title: Radar and sonar ranges
sections.body: radar_range matches the stated range for the basic radars (5000, 20000, 50000), sonars (3000, 1000), advanced sonars (60000, 100000, 200000) and the fish finder (100). The advanced radars without a stated range carry 60000 (radar), 500000 (AWACS), 200000 (dish), 100000 (phalanx) and 20000 (missile).

sections.title: Target signature
sections.body:
Every radar and sonar candidate test reads its signature S from the target's physics record, and that value is the mass of the target's physics body. Each component contributes its definition mass attribute through a shared getter, the vehicle code sums them per body and hands the sum to the physics object, and the sensors read it back. So S is mass in the game's definition mass units, not block count, area or hull length. More blocks raise S only through their mass.

A vehicle with several physics bodies presents one record per body, so the figures on this page apply to each body, not to the vehicle's total. The body sum also redistributes and clamps values and some components override the getter, so S is not always the plain sum of the definition masses.

sections.title: Advanced radar detection
sections.body:
The Basic, AWACS, Dish, Phalanx and Missile radars turn radar_range P into a working range R = P × 0.02 × 0.02 ÷ (FOV x × FOV y). FOV x and FOV y are 0.02 by default, and the editor sliders set each from 0.01 to 0.25 in steps of 0.01 (3.6 to 90 degrees). R is 4 × P at 0.01 per axis, equals radar_range at 0.02 and is 0.0064 × P at 0.25: the AWACS spans 2000000 m to 3200 m, the Missile 80000 m to 128 m. A new scan runs every N = max(1, floor(R ÷ 2000 + 0.5)) updates, at 60 updates per second.

A target of body mass S at distance d passes when d ≤ R and R ÷ 10000 × S ÷ d > 0.025, that is d < R × S ÷ 250. There is no random roll in this test. Each scan keeps at most 8 targets, best score first, and runs a line-of-sight query to each.

sections.title: Radar line of sight
sections.body: The line-of-sight query from the radar to each candidate filters objects by collision bits, not by what they look like. An object can block only when its collision group lacks bit 0x1000 and shares a bit with 0xff, and its object mask shares a bit with 0x7f. The target itself and objects with the same owner do not block. Whether glass, water, terrain or another vehicle carries those bits depends on how each is registered with the physics scene; render materials and transparency play no part in this test.

sections.title: Legacy radar and sonar detection
sections.body:
The six legacy parts (Radar, Radar (Dish), Radar (Large), Radar (Huge), Sonar (Large) and Sonar (Small); definition type 16, logic case 50) use a different test: a target passes when S ÷ d > 0.25, that is d < 4 × S. radar_range does not enter the score. It sets a far plane C = P × (0.75 + 0.25 × 0.01 ÷ saved radar_fov) ahead of the sensor, 0.775 × P at the saved default 0.1: 3875 m for the Radar, 15500 m for the Dish and Large, 38750 m for the Huge, 2325 m and 775 m for the sonars. On the sensor's axis a target passes within min(C, 4 × S); off the axis the straight-line distance can exceed C.

The FOV input is clamped to 0.01 to 0.125 turn (0.01 to 0.25 on the Large, which also uses it vertically; the others see 0.25 turn vertically). It moves the side planes only, because C reads the separately saved radar_fov field. Sonars run only at least 0.25 m below a sampled height and see targets reaching below y = -1; radars run only at least 0.25 m above it and see targets reaching above y = 1 (inference: the sampled height is the water surface). Candidates go best score first through a line-of-sight query; the Huge fills up to 8 targets and the others output one. The legacy sonars do not use the advanced sonar's ping or passive listening.

sections.title: Advanced sonar detection
sections.body:
Advanced sonars use radar_range as P. An active return passes when d ≤ P and P ÷ 10000 × S ÷ d > 0.01, that is d < P × S ÷ 100. After a ping, targets show up as an echo window moves out by 12.333333 m per update, 740 m per second.

While not pinging, a sonar hears other sonars' pings of amplitude 235 when 235 × P × 0.00002 ÷ d > 0.01, so one ping is heard within 0.47 × P. Targets whose directions differ by less than 0.01 in squared length merge, and at most 16 targets are output.

sections.title: Transponder locator pulses
sections.body: The locator takes the nearest beacon's 1 ÷ (0.002 d + 0.5), applies a small noise factor, clamps it to 0 to 1 and adds it to an accumulator each update. Each time the accumulator reaches 10 it pulses. Without noise that is 6 Hz within 250 m, 2.4 Hz at 1000 m and 0.2927 Hz at 10000 m. The noise factor comes from a shared counter, not from the beacon's position, and one factor multiplies the nearest beacon's term.

sections.title: Output noise
sections.body:
The game reads radar_noise, radar_distance_noise and sonar_noise from the SDK game_constants file. On the advanced radars and sonars, radar distances are multiplied by 1 − D + 2D U, and radar and sonar angles get −A + 2A U, with a fresh random U from 0 to 1 per value. At the defaults that is ±1% on distance and ±0.001 turn (±0.36 degrees) on each angle. Sonar outputs have no distance noise.

U comes from the shared random routine: state = 214013 × state + 2531011 modulo 2^32, which returns (state >> 16) & 32767, divided by 32767. So 2U − 1 takes 32768 equally spaced values from −1 to 1. Over the generator's full cycle each value occurs equally often, so the error is spread evenly across the band, not bell-shaped, and the draws follow a fixed sequence from the seed rather than being independent. The legacy radars and sonars add no noise: logic case 50 writes the geometric distance and angles straight to its outputs.

sections.title: Open questions
sections.body: Not decoded: how the body-mass producer's redistribution, clamping and linked bodies, and fuel, cargo or damage, change the signature S, and how S compares with the editor's mass total; which collision bits terrain, water, glass and vehicles register with, and so which of them block the line-of-sight query; the height sampler 0x1402bc7d0 behind the legacy height gates; what else can set a legacy sensor's saved radar_fov; what the legacy Signal Strength output carries; the laser missile radar (radar_type 2) acquisition path; advanced sonar submersion gating and the noisemaker's effect on the sonar. For radios: how the legacy radios' separate send and receive frequencies and their data use the receive routine, whose legacy records carry one frequency and no payload flags; payload and audio effects of a weak signal beyond the clamp(2 × S) level; the exact rounding of the native power routine in the height term. None of the radio figures was checked in a running game.

limitations: Signature S is the target's physics-body mass in game mass units, read per physics body. The open items about it are listed under Open questions.
Radio figures come from a static decode of the receive routine 0x14054a780; the radio items under Open questions are what it leaves open.
Unrelated definitions carry serialized default ranges; only sensor and radio definitions are interpreted here.

categories.summary: Propellers, rotors and ducted fans share one force-emitter update. Shaft speed and normalized pitch set a load that takes speed off the shaft and turns it into internal force T = 1500 × K × removed RPS × efficiency. force_emitter_max_force sets the solver weight K, not a thrust ceiling, and a separate 100 × S cap limits the applied force. Marine parts push only with the hub underwater, air parts only above it.

sections.title: Shared update
sections.body:
Each update the part reads its published shaft speed and computes w = RPS × 0.9999, the effective pitch p = clamp(saved pitch + input, -1, 1) and the load b = (2 × w × rotation_speed × π × blade_physics_length × p × 0.75 + p × U) × blade_efficiency × B × 0.32, where U is the relative flow along the thrust axis and B the number of intact blades. With q = clamp(b × 0.5 ÷ K, -10, 10), multiplied by 10 when the hub is below the water surface, it removes w × (1 - 1 ÷ (1 + q²)) RPS from its own speed and pushes with T = 1500 × K × removed RPS × efficiency, signed by the pitch.

The part submits K as its shaft weight together with the speed it kept on the previous update, so the shaft group feels the load one update later. At low speed in still air or water T grows about with RPS cubed; once q reaches its clamp it grows close to linearly. Zero pitch gives no load and no thrust, and negative pitch or RPS reverses the push.

sections.title: What force_emitter_max_force does
sections.body: K = F ÷ 1000. The pitchable marine propellers use K = F × B ÷ 8000 instead, F ÷ 2000 with 4 intact blades. Air parts use one of the two, chosen by a definition byte that the decode could not tie to a resource field, so their figures come in pairs. A larger F raises K, which lowers q, so less speed is removed per update while each removed RPS pushes harder. F ratios between sizes are therefore not thrust ratios, and raw force can exceed F: the small marine propeller (F = 20000) gives raw force 22201.426 at 10 RPS.

sections.title: Water and air
sections.body: The hub decides the medium: depth = hub height - sampled water surface. Marine parts push only at depth ≤ 0, air parts only at depth ≥ 0. Below the surface q is multiplied by 10 for every part, so a submerged rotor brakes its shaft far harder and, in this update, pushes not at all; the rotor tooltips call this decreased force. A dry marine propeller still loads its shaft. Air parts multiply T by P = (1 - 2.2413793e-5 × y)^5.3595023 of the body altitude y, 0 above 40000. Marine parts take U from their own velocity through still water, air parts from wind minus their velocity.

sections.title: Rotors, cyclic and reaction
sections.body: Roll and Pitch move the force point by -4 × input along local X and Z and tilt the push by 0.4 × input, which tips the vehicle without a blade-phase model. A physical rotor hinge gets a motor with impulse limit 1000 and a target speed from the shaft speed. Rotors with the coaxial flag add two opposite forces of 800 × b × clamp(|saved pitch + Collective + 0.1|, 0, 1), a moment about the rotor axis.

sections.title: Through-drive ports
sections.body: Rotors with Power Connection A and B link the two port nodes to each other. The shaft solver then mixes the two groups' speeds across that link with fraction 0.95 and ratio 1, as it does across a gearbox. The rotor's own load goes on A. The ports do not share a fixed part of the power and do not jump to one speed: groups of weight 11 at 10 RPS and 21 at rest publish 3.55412 and 3.322734 RPS.

sections.title: Application cap
sections.body: Every propeller, rotor and fan force is capped at 100 × S on its own, and solid rockets at 1000 × S. S is the summed adjusted mass of every body joined to this one by joints, free or locked, so all of them share one S; the Control surfaces category gives the rule and examples. Each force emitter also adds an auxiliary mass of 10 to the mass adjustment. That changes how the body masses are scaled, but it is not added to S.

sections.title: Rockets
sections.body: Solid rocket boosters burn once. Each update a nozzle of width w uses trunc(400 × w² × burn rate) + 1 fuel units and pushes with 60 times that, so a slower burn rate pushes less for longer, and fuel sections lengthen the burn without adding thrust.

sections.title: Open questions
sections.body: Not decoded: which loaded value sets the air weight selector byte (+0x580 behind the definition's first pointer) for each air part, so air figures stay in two branches; for the cap scale S, which code sets the assembly root flag (+0x29c) that drops the first body from the mass sum, and which connector links (connection records of kind 8) join bodies into one S group; the SI calibration of mass, force, torque and shaft power; the visible cyclic blade phase; the separate water-interaction helper 0x1402fe950, cavitation and other hydrodynamics outside the scalar law; whether anything elsewhere in the engine adds ground effect (the scalar law has no ground-clearance term); the editor-arrow sign table for reflected parts. No figure here was measured in a running game.

limitations: Static analysis of one build. Forces are in the game's internal force unit before the 100 × S application cap.

For active, normally simulated vehicles, these formulas run once per nominal 1/60-second simulation update. Multiply per-update amounts by 60 for amounts per simulated second. A constant relaxation fraction k leaves (1-k)^60 of a gap after one simulated second. Physics solver substeps and render frames are separate; pauses, sleeping, unloaded vehicles and real-time slowdown are outside this conversion.

categories.summary: Pilot seats expose four axes from −1 to 1, six hotkeys, look angles in turns and a composite with fixed channels (on/off 31 trigger, 32 occupied; values 1–4 axes, 9–10 look).

sections.title: Composite layout
sections.body: On/Off 1 and up carry hotkeys, 31 the trigger and 32 occupancy; values 1–4 carry the axes and 9–10 the look direction. The HOTAS seat adds axes 5–8 and up to 48 hotkeys.

limitations: Port descriptions only.

categories.summary: A firebox burns at most 0.00002 × voxels coal per update and heats its coolant; the boiler boils water at a fixed temperature of 100 at min(0.001 × (T - 100), water) per update; the turbine turns steam flow into a target RPS that keeps 0.985 per update, and the piston drives its crank by 0.002 × steam pressure difference × sin(2πz).

sections.title: Chain
sections.body: Coal from ducts and hoppers feeds the firebox. The firebox heats the fluid in its coolant chamber, which you circulate through the boiler's Coolant A and B. The boiler turns its water into steam for a turbine or pistons, and a condenser whose phase chamber is below 100 turns the exhaust back into water.

sections.title: Coal storage
sections.body: Ducts and hoppers add one item slot per voxel to the inventory they share with every connected firebox: 27, 125 and 225 for the small, medium and large sizes. Each firebox adds 10 more. Slots count whole items, and the firebox takes whole coal from them. The ducts' steam_component_capacity values 42.1875, 195.3125 and 351.5625 are 1.5625 times their voxel counts; the traced capacity code does not read them.

sections.title: Fireboxes
sections.body: Ignition takes one coal and sets the ignition state to 3600. The combustion code only tests whether that state is nonzero and never counts it down, so 3600 is not a burn time there. The fire also keeps burning while it is hotter than 150. When the fractional reserve is empty the firebox takes another coal and adds 1 to it. Each update it requests b = 0.00002 × voxels × clamp((600 - T) ÷ 400, 0, 1) coal, T being the fire temperature: at most 0.054 coal per simulated second for the small firebox and 0.21 for the large. Air limits the burn. A fraction u = clamp(r ÷ air amount, 0, 1) × clamp(P_air - 1 - P_exhaust, 0, 1) of the Air chamber moves to the Exhaust chamber, r = b × 200 ÷ 60, and the burn is cut to the share that oxygen covers at a 0.21 reference fraction. So it needs Air pressure more than 1 above Exhaust pressure. Burnt oxygen becomes carbon dioxide in the exhaust. Each unit of coal actually burned adds 200 to the fire temperature.

sections.title: Firebox heat and coolant
sections.body: The fire then loses 0.001 of its gap to the surrounding temperature per update, rising toward 0.01 with damage, and exchanges heat with its coolant chamber at k = 0.0008 × voxels: 0.036 small and 0.14 large. The fire counts with weight 400 and the coolant with its stored amount, and there is no exchange below 0.1 coolant. While burning, Air pulls air in with a bias of -10 and Exhaust pushes out with +10. With both coolant ports connected, Coolant In draws fluid with a bias of -clamp(T - 50, 0, 10), so a fire hotter than 50 drives its own coolant loop (inference from the port solver's sign).

sections.title: Boiling and condensing
sections.body: The boiler and condenser convert between water and steam in their phase chamber at a fixed temperature of 100, whatever the pressure. At or above 100, min(0.001 × (T - 100), water) of fresh and salt water becomes steam per update, 1:1 by stored amount, which is 0.06 × (T - 100) per simulated second until water runs short. Below 100, min(0.001 × (100 - T), 0.1 × steam) condenses into fresh water. Each step shifts the chamber temperature by only 0.01 × converted ÷ total amount, so boiling takes almost no heat from the water.

sections.title: Boiler and condenser heat transfer
sections.body: Each update the phase and coolant chambers exchange heat with k = 0.1 × (1 - D), D = clamp(0.1 × damage, 0, 1), each side moving by k times the other side's share of the liquid amount. The condenser counts its whole phase chamber, steam included. Both chambers then lose 0.0001 of their gap to the surroundings per update. The phase chamber holds 0.1 × voxels, 17.5 in the boiler and 7.5 in the condenser, and the coolant chamber 1 per voxel, 175 and 75.

sections.title: Turbines
sections.body: The turbine passes gas from Steam In to Steam Out one way, through the pump solver with flow factor 0.0025 and no bias, so it needs inlet pressure above exhaust pressure and consumes no steam. Each update it adds 1000 × the steam moved to its speed, 600 × when damaged and nothing at damage 20 or more, multiplies by 0.985 and submits the result as target RPS on both RPS ports with weight 65. The shaft group's speed then replaces the stored speed. Unloaded, a steady steam step q settles at 0.985 ÷ 0.015 × 1000 × q (inference). Pure steam networks of volume 4 at pressures 2 and 1 move at most (2 - 1) ÷ 24000 per update, which settles at 2.736111 RPS.

sections.title: Pistons
sections.body: Each piston has two chambers of 0.0015 × voxels. Its crank phase z, wrapped to 0 to 1, opens one port per chamber: from z = 0.5 the first Steam In and the second Steam Out, below 0.5 the first Steam Out and the second Steam In (port order taken from the definition, inference). Each update it adds a = 0.002 × (p_B - p_A) × sin(2πz) to its crank group, p being chamber pressure times its steam fraction. With steam on both Steam In ports and both Steam Out ports vented, the open chamber matches the sign of the sine on each half turn, so the drive keeps one direction (inference). Both RPS ports submit the group speed with weight 20 × voxels: 120, 1620 and 5700, and a connected port copies its shaft group's published speed back into the crank group.

sections.title: Crank groups
sections.body: At the end of each update every crank group adds the summed drive a to its speed, multiplies by 0.99, clamps the result to −10 … 10 and clears a. Its phase then advances by speed ÷ 60 turns and wraps with floor, so a crank turning backward wraps too, and the speed is in RPS, capped at 10. There is no division by an inertia sum: shaft load acts only through the port exchange, which replaces the group speed with the shaft group's published speed before this step. Unloaded, a constant drive a settles at 99 × a and reaches the cap from a = 0.10101.

sections.title: Open questions
sections.body: Ignition writes 3600 to a state that the recovered firebox combustion paths test as a nonzero enable. No countdown was found in those paths, and the complete gameplay writer that clears or decrements it was not traced. Hot damaged fireboxes can queue a component and body event when vehicle damage is on. The event consumer, any global blast and any pressure-triggered boiler rupture were not traced; no pressure limit or burst test appears in the boiler, condenser or phase code. Also not decoded: the unit steam_component_capacity once had, and any joule, N m or efficiency calibration of coal heat, turbine speed and piston drive.

limitations: Static analysis of one build. Temperatures, pressures, amounts and speeds are the game's internal values; no figure here was measured in a running game.

For active, normally simulated vehicles, these formulas run once per nominal 1/60-second simulation update. Multiply per-update amounts by 60 for amounts per simulated second. A constant relaxation fraction k leaves (1-k)^60 of a gap after one simulated second. Physics solver substeps and render frames are separate; pauses, sleeping, unloaded vehicles and real-time slowdown are outside this conversion.

categories.summary: Weight blocks shift the centre of mass. Keels push against sideways water speed, add a fixed downward force while immersed and turn themselves back toward vertical, which is what lets sails drive a boat across or into the wind.

sections.title: Keels
sections.body: Under water a keel's sideways force is 40 × u × min(0.5 × M, 400) × w × 10, u being the sideways water speed clamped to ±50 m/s, M the body mass and w the immersion; every size has the same law. A fixed downward force of 1000 acts whenever the keel is immersed. The self-righting torque 800 × K × w × |sin θ| grows with size: K = min(S, 4 × definition mass) reaches 2000, 4000 and 8000. The Keel page has the full decode.

sections.title: Skis
sections.body: Skis slide lengthwise and grip laterally.

limitations: Weight block and ski guidance rests on tooltip statements.
Keel figures come from static analysis of one build; their open questions are listed on the Keel page.

categories.summary: Gearboxes pull RPS B toward the selected ratio × RPS A, so for an N:1 option RPS A is the fast side. Ratio changes apply at once while the gearbox has power, and a bridge mixes the two shaft groups' speeds by solver weight with no slip threshold.

sections.title: Ratio orientation
sections.body: Both ratios are chosen from eight fixed options, not typed numbers: 1:-1, 1:1, 6:5, 3:2, 9:5, 2:1, 5:2 and 3:1. Each option is a multiplier q: -1, 1, 0.8333333, 0.6666667, 0.5555556, 0.5, 0.4 and 0.33333334. The gearbox stores q on its RPS A connection and 1 ÷ q on RPS B, and the shaft solver pulls RPS B toward q × RPS A. For an N:1 option RPS A is therefore the fast side: at 3:1 with RPS A at 30, RPS B is pulled toward 10. At 6:5 RPS A turns 6/5 as fast as RPS B. 1:-1 targets the same speed with the opposite sign.

sections.title: Coupling
sections.body:
RPS A and RPS B stay two separate shaft groups joined by a bridge. Each update every group first mixes its own parts: weight I = 1 + Σ F and speed v = (previous speed + Σ F × submitted speed) ÷ I, with F each part's submitted solver weight. The bridge then adds the other group's speed with path weight h = 0.95 × c, where c is the bridge fraction, 1 for an intact gearbox. A path from A adds sign(q) × v_A × I_A × h to B's numerator and I_A × h ÷ |q| to B's weight; paths with h at or below 0.001 add nothing. For two groups this gives B' = (I_B v_B + sign(q) I_A v_A h) ÷ (I_B + I_A h ÷ |q|) and A' = (I_A v_A + sign(q) I_B v_B h) ÷ (I_A + I_B h |q|).

Two groups already at the ratio stay there, so 0.95 weakens the coupling weight and is not a 95% power efficiency or a 5% speed loss. There is no slip threshold: under load the two sides settle where the weights balance. Example from rest, A with one part of weight 200 at 30 RPS (v_A 29.85, I_A 201) and B with one part of weight 100 at 0 RPS (I_B 101): one pass at 3:1 gives A 25.75 and B 8.459 RPS.

sections.title: Several bridges and loops
sections.body:
Each update every group first mixes its own parts. Then every group in turn acts as a source s and sends its speed through the bridges once. A queue starts with its bridge partners in member order. Each entry carries the path weight h, multiplied by 0.95 × bridge fraction per link, and the cumulative ratio r; entries with h at or below 0.001 stop. The first time a group is reached it gets sign(r) × v_s × I_s × h on its numerator and I_s × h ÷ |r| on its weight, and its own bridges join the queue.

A group reached again by another path compares the recorded ratio with the new one. If recorded ÷ new lies within 0.9 to 1.1 the path is skipped, so a consistent loop passes each source's speed once, along the first path in queue order. Otherwise the ratios contradict. Every group this source has reached loses all bridge shares gathered so far, including those from earlier sources, gains I_s of weight with no speed, and the source stops. Later sources can add shares again, so the outcome depends on the group order, and a contradicting loop acts as a brake rather than settling on one speed.

A bridge with both ports on one group is checked against ratio 1. A 1:1 link adds nothing. Inference from the comparison: any other option, such as 2:1, brakes the group, and an otherwise isolated group then publishes v ÷ 2, 5 RPS from 10. After all sources each group publishes once; there is no iteration toward a converged speed. The source order is the order of the group container, not component IDs.

sections.title: Shaft group rebuild
sections.body: A rebuild first resets every component, which clears each registered shaft connection's group pointer, submitted weight and speed and published speed. Only then are the old groups freed. The builder then starts a new group at speed 0 and weight 1 for each connection not yet in a group and appends members in the order component enumeration and connection traversal reach them; nothing sorts them by position or speed. A group with fewer than 2 members is dropped. That discovery order is the member and queue order the bridge traversal above follows.

sections.title: Switching and power
sections.body: Gear Switch off applies Ratio Off and on applies Ratio On. When the selected q differs from the stored one by more than 0.001, both stored ratios are replaced in the same update, with no interpolation or delay, and the gearbox requests 0.001 electricity. This only happens while max(0, (300 - EMP count) ÷ 300) × charge fraction is above 0, or with infinite electricity. Without power the gearbox keeps its last ratio and stays coupled: the bridge fraction is set to 1 every update before the power test.

sections.title: Damage
sections.body: Any nonzero damage sets both bridge fractions to 0 every update, so a damaged gearbox or clutch disconnects its two sides. Gearboxes and clutches use the shared damage setter, which stores at most 50. The shared repair routine lowers damage by an amount its caller passes, never below 0, and at 0 the next update couples the two sides again.

sections.title: Torque meter readings
sections.body: A torque meter's RPS output copies the group speed. Its Torque output is the group's effective solver weight I + D, not newton-metres, so meters on both sides of a gearbox or clutch do not measure the torque it transmits.

sections.title: Standalone clutch
sections.body: The standalone clutch uses the same bridge at ratio 1 with c = e × clamp(Clutch Pressure, 0, 1)^6, set directly each update. e = min(1, availability ÷ 0.01), so 1% supply already gives full strength. Input 0.5 gives c = 1/64; an isolated clutch couples nothing below input 0.3189. The modular engine clutch is a different part with a cubed target and a 0.1 per update slew.

limitations: SI torque, inertia and physical power losses are unknown: the bridge is a weighted speed exchange in solver units, and no conversion to newton-metres or watts was recovered. No finite slip torque or friction law was recovered.

torque_gearbox_2's tooltip claims a torque-difference limit of 4000, but its enforcing path and internal unit were not established. The recovered gearbox update, ratio helper and shaft solver hold no 4000 and compare the copied force_emitter_max_force with nothing.

Damage disables the gearbox or clutch bridge. Both use the shared capped damage setter, and the shared repair routine can subtract damage to 0. The complete damage triggers, repair cadence and any torque-triggered breakage were not traced.

The rebuild clears registered shaft-node group pointers before freeing the old groups, then forms new groups and appends members in connection-discovery order. Which connector changes schedule a rebuild, and the update ordering that would rule out a pass on stale membership, were not traced, so the braking outcome of a contradicting loop after a rebuild is not predicted.
Static analysis only.

For active, normally simulated vehicles, these formulas run once per nominal 1/60-second simulation update. Multiply per-update amounts by 60 for amounts per simulated second. A constant relaxation fraction k leaves (1-k)^60 of a gap after one simulated second. Physics solver substeps and render frames are separate; pauses, sleeping, unloaded vehicles and real-time slowdown are outside this conversion.

categories.summary: Each gun fires from a fixed per-class record: 800 to 1000 m/s for the machine gun and autocannons and 600 to 800 m/s for the cannons, added to the firing body's velocity. Rounds keep a fixed fraction of their velocity each update and fall at 30 m/s² at sea level. Barrel extensions narrow the spread, not the muzzle speed, and a gun stops at heat 1 until it cools below 0.25.

sections.title: Gun classes
sections.body: weapon_class selects one row of a 7-row native table, and that row names the projectile row: Machine Gun 800 m/s, keeps 0.975 per update, removed after 300 updates; Light Autocannon 1000 m/s, keeps 0.98 per update, removed after 300 updates; Rotary Autocannon 1000 m/s, keeps 0.99 per update, removed after 300 updates; Heavy Autocannon 900 m/s, keeps 0.995 per update, removed after 600 updates; Battle Cannon 800 m/s, keeps 0.998 per update, removed after 3600 updates; Artillery Cannon 700 m/s, keeps 0.999 per update, removed after 3600 updates; Bertha Cannon 600 m/s, keeps 0.9995 per update, removed after 3600 updates. weapon_barrel_length_voxels is not part of the velocity: V = muzzle speed × direction + firing body velocity.

sections.title: Flight
sections.body:
Each update a round first moves by its velocity ÷ 60, then loses 0.5 × (138750 ÷ (138750 + y))² m/s of vertical speed, y being its height above sea level, then keeps a fixed fraction r of its velocity. That is 30 m/s² of gravity at sea level, and r is a linear retention per update, not a speed-squared drag law. Under water the gravity step is 0.2 and r is multiplied by 0.8. Machine-gun and autocannon rounds are removed once they slow below 50 m/s; battle, artillery and Bertha shells skip that test until they are in water. Every round is removed at the end of its lifetime.

Fired level from 1 m above a flat plane at sea level, a rotary autocannon round lands 253.9 m out after 0.27 s. At 20° a battle cannon shell lands 5161.3 m out after 14.46 s, and at 45° a Bertha shell 7606.4 m out after 25.72 s. A machine-gun round at 5° slows below 50 m/s after about 500 m and is removed in the air.

sections.title: Spread and barrel extensions
sections.body: The firing direction turns by two independent random angles, each uniform within ±0.25 × dispersion × m radians. Dispersion is 0.01 for the machine gun, light and heavy autocannon and battle cannon, 0.02 for the rotary autocannon and 0.005 for the artillery and Bertha cannons, so a bare gun spreads ±0.0025, ±0.005 or ±0.00125 rad per axis. m starts at 1 and each barrel extension of the gun's class subtracts 0.2, down to 0.5: one extension gives 0.8, two 0.6, three or more 0.5. Extensions and muzzle brakes move the muzzle forward by 0.25 per voxel of their length; muzzle brakes do not change m, and nothing in the walk changes muzzle speed.

sections.title: Recoil
sections.body: A shot submits F = -50 × recoil coefficient × multiplier × V for one update, V being the projectile's velocity. The gun constructor sets the multiplier to 1 and both firing branches read it unchanged. The coefficients run 0.1, 0.2, 0.3, 0.5, 2, 4 and 8 from the machine gun to the Bertha, so a stationary gun pushes back with 4000, 10000, 15000, 22500, 80000, 140000, 240000 internal force units in that order. Barrel extensions do not change the coefficient or the multiplier; their added mass changes how the vehicle responds.

sections.title: Impact and explosions
sections.body: The impact magnitude M is B × speed ÷ 1000 for kinetic rounds, 0.4 times that for armour-piercing and 0.65 times that for incendiary. High explosive uses M = B and fragmentation 0.4 × B, where the projectile supports explosives; the machine-gun round does not. B is 0.1, 0.2, 0.3, 0.6, 1, 2 and 4 from the machine gun to the Bertha. Explosions search within 7.5 × M m and push with up to 50000 × M before caps, and fragmentation rounds also release 2 to 80 fragments. An armour-piercing round loses 100 × p × mass ÷ cells of speed per component cell it passes, keeping its direction. These magnitudes are inputs to the damage routines, not hit points.

sections.title: Timed fuses
sections.body: Fuse Timer is read for fragmentation rounds on any gun that fires them and for high-explosive rounds on the heavy autocannon and the cannons. A positive input sets T = max(1/60, input + 0.02 × u - 0.01) s, u random from 0 to 1. The round detonates in the update where (age + 1) ÷ 60 reaches T, at a point interpolated within that update. The lifetime or the 50 m/s removal can end the flight first.

sections.title: Loading and firing rate
sections.body: Breech transitions take 2, 4, 1, 16, 75, 250 and 600 updates from the machine gun to the Bertha. After a round arrives the receiver waits 30, 90 and 240 updates on the battle, artillery and Bertha cannons, 6 for heavy autocannon rounds and none otherwise. Inference from that state machine, not a measurement: with a round always ready the automatic guns cycle every 2 × transition + delay updates, 900, 450, 1800 and 94.737 rounds per minute for the machine gun, light, rotary and heavy autocannon. Drums hold their full weapon_ammo_capacity of light rounds, half of it in rotary rounds and a fifth in heavy rounds: light 100/200/500; rotary 50/100/250; heavy 20/40/100 rounds.

sections.title: Heat
sections.body: Every gun adds its heat per shot, 0.0125, 0.025, 0.01, 0.08 and 0.02 for the machine gun, light, rotary and heavy autocannon and the three cannons. Each update then removes 0.002, 0.12 per second. At heat 1 the gun stops firing until heat drops below 0.25. Inference with ideal feeding and the trigger held: the rotary autocannon stops on shot 166, the light autocannon on shot 110 and the machine gun on shot 221.

sections.title: Open questions
sections.body: Not decoded: a throughput model for arbitrary belt networks, combining direction, order, junctions and neighbour search; the fastest schedule for cannons whose breech is opened and loaded by external control; and what follows the decoded impact magnitude and armour-piercing speed loss: the target voxel damage, the armour-angle response and blast shielding. No direct write to the recoil multiplier besides its initial 1 was found, so the reduction a muzzle brake's tooltip promises is not established. No figure here was measured in a running game.

limitations: Static analysis of one build. Forces and impact magnitudes are internal units.

For active, normally simulated vehicles, these formulas run once per nominal 1/60-second simulation update. Multiply per-update amounts by 60 for amounts per simulated second. A constant relaxation fraction k leaves (1-k)^60 of a gap after one simulated second. Physics solver substeps and render frames are separate; pauses, sleeping, unloaded vehicles and real-time slowdown are outside this conversion.

categories.summary: The tyre surface moves at 2π × r × RPS m/s with r = wheel_radius - 0.125 + 0.125 × wheel_size metres. Grip pulls ground and tread speed together from bounded slip, and the wheel feeds its RPS back into the shaft.

sections.title: Speed per RPS
sections.body: Road and tank wheels run one update. Its working radius is r = wheel_radius - 0.125 + 0.125 × wheel_size in metres, and the tyre surface moves at 2π × r × RPS m/s. wheel_size starts at 1, which leaves r = wheel_radius. At that size the 3x3, 5x5, 7x7 and 9x9 wheels give 2.199, 3.644, 5.341 and 6.597 m/s per RPS (7.917, 13.12, 19.23 and 23.75 km/h), with or without suspension. Tank wheels give 2.513 m/s per RPS for the small sizes, 3.927 for medium and large and 6.283 for huge. Each 0.1 of wheel_size adds 0.0125 m to r. A vehicle reaches this speed only while its wheels do not slip.

sections.title: Grip
sections.body: Each wheel casts a ray to the ground and also has a sphere body with friction 0.001. From the ray hit the update takes the velocity of the ground point relative to the tyre point, tread speed included, scales it down to 5 m/s when longer and drops its part along the ray. That slip u asks for Q = (50 × grip_factor × tyre factor ÷ r) × (2000 q + 100 u), where q is the drift of the contact point since the last update, multiplied by the brake and at most 0.1 × r. Forward and sideways slip share one gain, and no normal load enters it. The tyre factor starts at 1, 1.75 for a double wheel, and is multiplied by 0.25, 0.1875 or 0.125 for tyre type 0, 1 or 2. For a Wheel 3x3 with the default type 1 that is 2678.571 internal units per m/s of slip, capped by the 5 m/s limit. Q is an internal impulse request that the impulse helpers scale and cap with a factor B before it reaches a body, so it is not a force in newtons.

sections.title: Shaft feedback and braking
sections.body: Contact also corrects the wheel's RPS: it adds (slip along the tyre) ÷ (2π × r) × tyre factor × grip_factor × 0.5, which moves the RPS toward the ground speed (inference from the sign of the slip term). The wheel then joins its shaft group like any member, submitting that RPS with a weight equal to its definition mass, × 0.7 for wheels with suspension: 10, 20, 40 and 80 without suspension and 10.5, 21, 42 and 84 with it. It takes the group speed back. So a slipping wheel drags on the engine and a coasting vehicle drives the shaft (inference); there is no fixed gear between shaft and ground. Finally the RPS is multiplied by 1 - brake and by a retention: 0.99 for tyre type 0, 0.995 for type 1, 1 for type 2.

sections.title: Suspension springs
sections.body: Wheels with suspension push the chassis along the ray with 60 × tyre_pressure × (k × max(0, r + 0.5 × r - l) + c × (l_old - l)), l being the ray distance, k = 0.05 + 0.45 × stiffness_factor and c = 0.5 + 4.5 × damping_factor: 0.23 and 0.995 at the defaults 0.4 and 0.11. Wheels without suspension carry flag 0x800000, which sets k and c to 0, so this chassis spring adds nothing, and sets L = 0.3 × r and a = 0.8 × r. A second request, 60 × tyre_pressure × (max(0, 0.2 × r + a - l) + 4 × (l_old - l)), uses the hit body's own scale and runs in both. Both are internal requests that the helpers scale by B again, and the wheel's sphere body also collides normally.

sections.title: Tracks
sections.body: Tank wheels in one track share speed by a plain mean: the track pass adds each member's signed RPS, divides by the count and writes the mean back to every member. Two members at 10 and 0 RPS both leave at 5, whatever their radii, so tank wheels of different sizes in one track turn at one RPS but their treads move at different speeds. A tank wheel keeps its tyre factor 1 inside a track and halves it outside one, and keeps 0.975 of its RPS per update in a track and 0.7 outside one; the tyre type is ignored.

sections.title: Gravity, damping and contact friction
sections.body: The physics world is a Bullet btSoftRigidDynamicsWorld with a btSequentialImpulseConstraintSolver. World gravity is (0, -10, 0) m/s² with Y up, and each vehicle passes its configured gravity, 10 by default, to its bodies. The solver runs fixed substeps at 60, 120 or 180 Hz, up to 1000 per tick, while components update 60 times per simulated second. Each solver step multiplies a body's velocity by (1 - d)^dt with d clamped to 0 to 1, so the default vehicle damping 0.1 keeps 0.9 of the speed per simulated second at any solver rate. Vehicle linear damping is also multiplied by (1 - 0.0000224138 × y)^5.3595 and is 0 above y = 40000 (inference: y is height in metres). Bullet contact friction is clamp(μA × μB, -10, 10): 0.64 for two vehicle bodies at the default 0.8 and 0.0008 for a wheel's sphere body on a vehicle, so wheels get their grip from the ray request, not from the body contact.

sections.title: Open questions
sections.body: Not measured: vehicle speed and slip under load in a running game. Not recovered: the physical scale B the impulse helpers apply, so wheel grip has no newton or N m figure and no load curve; what sets the physics mode byte that gates the spring requests, and the other contact cases; how wheels are grouped into tracks, what Track Tension changes and how the belt touches the ground; what reads the track mean of component+0x808; and the speed law of the legacy Small, Medium and landing wheels, which run a separate update.

limitations: Static analysis of one build. Tread speeds are the no-slip speed of the tyre surface; no vehicle speed, slip or force was measured in a running game.

For active, normally simulated vehicles, these formulas run once per nominal 1/60-second simulation update. Multiply per-update amounts by 60 for amounts per simulated second. Physics solver substeps and render frames are separate; pauses, sleeping, unloaded vehicles and real-time slowdown are outside this conversion.

categories.summary: All 41 windows are plain type-9 parts: the factory gives them the shared basic component class, which has no per-update callback, and their definitions carry ordinary collision voxels and buoyancy surfaces.

sections.title: Component class
sections.body: Every window definition has type 9, the same type as 18 other parts (linear modules, railings, stairs and tyres). The component factory gives type 9 the basic class; its 88 vtable slots stop before the per-update slot that active parts use, so a window runs no code of its own. A type-9 test alone cannot pick out glass.

sections.title: Collision and buoyancy
sections.body: Window voxels have flags 1, like a plain block's voxel. Window 1x1 has 1 voxel and 1 buoyancy surface, Window 3x3 9 and 9, Porthole 15 voxels and 46 surfaces; the plain Block has 1 voxel and 6 surfaces. Transparent parts do not drop collision or buoyancy data.

sections.title: Placement
sections.body: Flat windows sit flush with walls; angled and corner pieces close gaps between angled windows.

limitations: Windows have ordinary collision voxels and explicit buoyancy surfaces, and glass is a named material, but whether damage breaks window glass and whether broken glass changes sealing, flooding, pressure or buoyancy were not traced; no glass-breaking threshold or window pressure rule is known.

The search covered every window definition, the type-9 class and its vtable, and executable strings. The glass references 0x140680528 and 0x14068a0e8 are rendering candidates; 0x1407a6c46 registers glass as material 35, and the physics flood string labels an editor option, so neither is a damage or flooding branch. Static analysis of one build; the game was not run.

families.summary: Mixes two gas compartments of 20, 250 or 1215 L each, moving 0.03 of the gap per update weighted by stored gas amount, which rises with pressure.

sections.title: Operating conditions
sections.body: Case 0x11 uses the gas capacity helper for both sides: q is the stored amount of the air slot, CO2, steam, oxygen, nitrogen and hydrogen, each with weight 1. Liquid in a side counts 0. Each side passes gas only with both its In and Out ports connected.

sections.title: Performance drivers
sections.body: The per-update rule is the same as for the other exchangers: 0.03 of the gap, weighted by the opposite side's share of q, plus a 0.001 drift toward ambient. Without through-flow, 0.161 of the gap remains after one simulated second.

sections.title: Gas pressure
sections.body: For pure gas q = P × V ÷ 60, so doubling a side's pressure doubles its q and the lower-pressure side moves further toward the other. The helper adds no pressure or temperature factor of its own. If a side also holds liquid, its q is the gas amount alone, not P × V ÷ 60.

sections.title: Variant tradeoffs
sections.body: The 2x2, 2x5 and 3x9 hold 2, 25 and 121.5 volume units per side (20, 250 and 1215 L), ratios 1, 12.5 and 60.75. The files are named heat_exchanger_2_2, heat_exchanger_5_5 and heat_exchanger_9_9; the listed voxel count, not the name, sets the volume.

sections.title: Flow example
sections.body: The 2x2 at 30 atm with 600 L/s of expanded gas through each side, inlets 100 and 20 °C and ambient 20 °C, emits 71.55 and 43.86 °C. Temp A and Temp B settle at 71.08 and 44.25 °C. These are outputs of the report's 60 Hz model with fixed boundary networks and a prescribed flow, not game measurements or a pump rating. The interactive graph below runs the same model.

sections.title: Setup and interactions
sections.body: Temp A and Temp B read the stored compartment temperatures in °C after this update's exchange and ambient step. Fluid leaving the Out ports was emitted earlier in the same update, so its temperature can differ. Both compartments also drift toward the surrounding temperature by 0.001 per update, so an idle exchanger slowly settles to ambient: the leak alone has a time constant of 16.7 simulated seconds.

findings.value: pure gas q = P × V ÷ 60; liquid q = stored liquid amount

At equal volume a 1 atm gas side has V ÷ 60 and a full liquid side V; at 60 atm the gas side equals the full liquid side. limitations: The exchanged quantity is a native amount × temperature unit; no conversion to joules or watts was recovered. No installation-independent effectiveness curve exists in the code: outlet temperatures depend on actual flow, fill, gas pressure, ambient and the connected networks.

For active, normally simulated vehicles, these formulas run once per nominal 1/60-second simulation update. Multiply per-update amounts by 60 for amounts per simulated second. A constant relaxation fraction k leaves (1-k)^60 of a gap after one simulated second. Physics solver substeps and render frames are separate; pauses, sleeping, unloaded vehicles and real-time slowdown are outside this conversion.

families.summary: Mixes a gas compartment and a liquid compartment of 10 to 1125 L each, moving 0.03 of the gap per update weighted by stored gas and liquid amount.

sections.title: Operating conditions
sections.body: Case 0x12 of the fluid-component update treats side A as gas (Air In/Air Out) and side B as liquid (Fluid In/Fluid Out): qA is the stored gas amount and qB the stored liquid amount. A side passes fluid only when its In and Out ports are both connected; the A/B exchange runs whenever qA + qB > 0.001, with or without flow. Neither side has a species filter or a pump bias, so fluid can run either way through a port pair.

sections.title: Performance drivers
sections.body: Per update, A moves toward B by 0.03 × qB ÷ (qA + qB) and B toward A by 0.03 × qA ÷ (qA + qB). The air side holds q = P × V ÷ 60 and the liquid side its stored liquid, so below 60 atm the liquid usually has the larger q and the air moves further toward it. With no through-flow and no ambient leak, 0.161 of the gap remains after one simulated second (60 updates).

sections.title: Variant tradeoffs
sections.body: All five variants share the 0.03 fraction. Each side holds 10, 50, 225, 405 or 1125 L (V = 1, 5, 22.5, 40.5 and 112.5), so at equal liquid fill and gas pressure both q values scale by 1, 5, 22.5, 40.5 and 112.5 relative to the 1x2. The fraction of the gap closed per update does not change. At equal external flow a larger variant also holds more fluid and loses more to ambient, so the volume ratio is not an outlet-temperature ratio.

sections.title: Flow example
sections.body: The 1x2 with 100 °C air at 30 atm and 600 L/s of expanded gas on side A, and 20 °C liquid at 0.8 fill and 6 L/s on side B, ambient 20 °C, emits air at 79.80 °C and liquid at 47.71 °C. Temp A and Temp B settle at 79.15 and 48.06 °C. These are outputs of the report's 60 Hz model with fixed boundary networks and a prescribed flow, not game measurements or a pump rating. The interactive graph below runs the same model.

sections.title: Setup and interactions
sections.body: Temp A and Temp B read the stored compartment temperatures in °C after this update's exchange and ambient step. Fluid leaving the Out ports was emitted earlier in the same update, so its temperature can differ. Both compartments also drift toward the surrounding temperature by 0.001 per update, so an idle exchanger slowly settles to ambient: the leak alone has a time constant of 16.7 simulated seconds.

findings.label: Exchanger capacity q
findings.value: pure gas q = P × V ÷ 60; liquid q = stored liquid amount
findings.detail: q is the side's stored amount of its phase in native units, 10 L of liquid or 600 L of expanded gas per amount. Inference from the pressure law: pure gas has P = 60 × G ÷ V, so q = G = P × V ÷ 60 and doubling pressure doubles q at a fixed volume. At equal volume a 1 atm gas side has V ÷ 60 and a full liquid side V; at 60 atm the gas side equals the full liquid side. With gas and liquid in one side, sum the gas amounts instead of using P × V ÷ 60. Wrong-phase contents give 0 toward that side's q but still move through the ports. Report: investigation/heat-exchangers.md. limitations: The exchanged quantity is a native amount × temperature unit; no conversion to joules or watts was recovered. No installation-independent effectiveness curve exists in the code: outlet temperatures depend on actual flow, fill, gas pressure, ambient and the connected networks.

For active, normally simulated vehicles, these formulas run once per nominal 1/60-second simulation update. Multiply per-update amounts by 60 for amounts per simulated second. A constant relaxation fraction k leaves (1-k)^60 of a gap after one simulated second. Physics solver substeps and render frames are separate; pauses, sleeping, unloaded vehicles and real-time slowdown are outside this conversion.

families.summary: Holds 100, 200 or 500 light autocannon rounds, half as many rotary rounds and a fifth as many heavy rounds.

sections.title: Capacity by calibre
sections.body: The store counts its five damage-kind bins against weapon_ammo_capacity, halved for rotary rounds and divided by 5 for heavy rounds: light 100/200/500; rotary 50/100/250; heavy 20/40/100 rounds.

sections.title: Feeding
sections.body: A round moves into a gun only while the gun's breech and receiver timers are 0 and the calibres match. The heavy autocannon then waits 6 updates before the next transition.

sections.title: Capacity
sections.body: Ducts, hoppers and fireboxes connected together share one inventory. Each duct adds its voxel count in item slots, 27, 125 or 225, each hopper the same, and each firebox 10. The firebox takes whole coal from it.

families.summary: rudder_surface_area 2, 8 and 12; deflects up to 0.25 rad, about 14.3°, each way.

sections.title: Variant tradeoffs
sections.body: Force scales linearly with rudder_surface_area, so medium and large fins make 4 and 6 times the force of the small one under the same conditions. Fins have smaller area and deflection than control surfaces, suiting fine trim.

sections.title: Air force
sections.body: Fins use the same routine as control surfaces, with rudder_type 0 and no wing term: force = 24 × area × P × B × (1 - immersion) × (airspeed - 15) × normal airspeed, above 15 m/s.

Which visible edge and editor arrow match positive deflection was not checked in game.

families.summary: rudder_surface_area 10, 28 and 70; deflects up to 0.785398 rad, about 45°, each way.

sections.title: Variant tradeoffs
sections.body: Force scales linearly with rudder_surface_area, so medium and large surfaces make 2.8 and 7 times the force of the small one under the same conditions. All sizes share the 45° limit and the -1 to 1 Rotation input.

sections.title: Air force
sections.body: Control surfaces have rudder_type 0, so there is no wing term: force = 24 × area × P × B × (1 - immersion) × (airspeed - 15) × normal airspeed, above 15 m/s. A surface edge-on to the airflow makes no force.

sections.title: Deflection speed
sections.body: Moving the surface draws electricity in proportion to the requested change. With full supply it reaches the requested angle in one update; with partial supply it moves part of the way.

families.summary: Small, medium and large diesel engines share one update: shaft weight 10, 30 and 100 and diesel use in the ratio 1 : 3 : 10 at the same RPS and throttle, with 0.102857, 0.308571 and 1.028571 L/s at 10 RPS and full throttle.

sections.title: Operating conditions
sections.body: Throttle is clamped to 0 to 1; a negative value counts as 0, so the engine never drives backward. Above the RPS Limiter (default 20 RPS, editor range 5 to 100) the throttle is cut to 0. That is a fuel cut, not a speed clamp: the engine can overshoot, and another component can spin the shaft faster. A damaged engine compares against 1.25 times the limit. Max Power (0 to 100 %) scales diesel use, intake and shaft weight together. Holding Starter draws electricity and pushes the engine toward 5 RPS. Fuel, air, cold and hot coolant and exhaust each have their own connection; the RPS and Temperature outputs report the engine's speed and temperature.

sections.title: Variant tradeoffs
sections.body: engine_max_force F is 20000, 60000 and 200000 for the small, medium and large diesel. The update uses it as a shaft weight W = F × Max Power ÷ 2000 (10, 30 and 100), as the diesel and intake demand scale s = F × Max Power ÷ 20000 (1, 3 and 10), and in the starter's charge request. At the same RPS and throttle every size gains speed and heats at the same rate. The bigger engine counts 3 or 10 times as much in the shaft's weighted average, so it holds speed better under load, and burns 3 or 10 times the diesel. W and the speed steps are internal solver quantities, not N m, watts or joules.

sections.title: Speed, fuel and heat
sections.body:
With local speed r in RPS and effective throttle u, the speed factor is g(r) = 1 ÷ (0.03 × r + 0.05) + 0.4 × r - 6. Diesel use is 0.012 × s × u × r × g(r) L/s. At full throttle and 10 RPS that is 0.102857, 0.308571 and 1.028571 L/s for the small, medium and large engine; at 20 RPS 0.849231, 2.547692 and 8.492308 L/s, so fuel use climbs steeply with speed. u is the throttle after the limiter and EMP cuts, reduced further when diesel, oxygen or the intake-over-exhaust pressure margin runs short. Full throttle needs air with 21 % oxygen and an intake pressure at least 2 above the exhaust; at a margin of 1 or less the engine gets no air. With infinite_fuel on, the diesel, air and exhaust exchange is skipped.

Each update the engine submits r_submit = 0.99 × (r + 0.1 × u × (r + 1)) to its shaft. Combustion adds speed only above 2 RPS; below that only the 0.99 retention applies, although the fuel formula still runs. At 10 RPS and full throttle the submitted speed is 10.989 RPS. Combustion outpaces the 1 % loss at every speed once u is about 0.101 or more, so an engine with nothing else on its shaft speeds up until the limiter cuts the throttle. The limiter, not the throttle, sets its free-running speed.

Heating is 0.0075 × |r| °C per update, 0.45 × |r| per simulated second, before cooling: 4.5 °C/s at 10 RPS for every size. It does not depend on throttle directly, so a shaft driven by another engine heats this one at zero throttle.

sections.title: Shaft and load
sections.body: The engine writes W and r_submit to its shaft group and takes back the group speed. A simple group mixes (R + Σ W_i × r_i) ÷ (1 + Σ W_i), where R is the group's previous speed. Several engines on one shaft therefore pull it toward their submitted speeds in proportion to W. The RPS output shows the local speed entering the update, before this update's starter and combustion steps.

sections.title: Reverse rotation and invalid speeds
sections.body:
The limiter and the combustion gate compare signed speed. A shaft turning backward never trips the throttle cut and never gets combustion gain, so the engine's own candidate is 0.99 × r: at −10 RPS it submits −9.9 and decays toward 0 unless the shaft keeps driving it. Heating uses |r|, so backward rotation heats the engine as much as forward rotation. The fuel curve g(r) uses signed speed, so the forward fuel figures above do not carry over to reverse speeds.

The speed branch does not replace NaN or infinity. NaN and −infinity skip combustion and stay as they are after the 0.99 factor; +infinity stays +infinity, or becomes NaN at zero effective throttle below damage 20. A connected shaft then replaces the local speed with its group's published speed.

sections.title: Cooling and overheating
sections.body:
Each engine holds 100 L of fresh water coolant at start. Each update the coolant ports exchange fluid, then engine and coolant move toward each other: with liquid coolant they meet halfway (factor 0.5), with gas or empty coolant not at all. The engine then moves 0.001 of the way toward the surrounding temperature, which it samples every 16 updates with the heat exchangers' routine and ramps over 16 updates. Outside a compartment that sample is the weather temperature: dry sea-level air from −15 °C to 30 °C depending on region, season and time of day, 6.5 °C colder per 1000 m of height, lower in rain, and water below the surface; the Weather temperature, lighting and hazards mechanics article gives the equations. The hot output gets a pump bias of 0.1 × |r|, at most 2; the cold return has none. Example: everything at 20 °C, 10 RPS, liquid coolant: the engine ends the update at 20.0374625 °C instead of 20.074925 °C without coolant.

Above 115 °C, with the engine_overheating and vehicle_damage settings both on, the engine takes 1 damage at once and 1 more every 300 updates (5 simulated seconds), up to 50. Turning off either setting stops overheat damage; the temperature still rises. Damage 1 to 19 cuts the combustion gain from 0.1 to 0.06; from 20 combustion adds no speed while fuel and heat continue.

sections.title: Starter
sections.body: While Starter is held the engine requests max(5 - r, 0) × W × electric_magnitude × 0.1 charge: 1.2, 3.6 and 12 per RPS below 5 for the small, medium and large engine, 6, 18 and 60 from rest. It adds the supplied fraction of the deficit to its speed, so full supply lifts it to 5 RPS in one update before shaft mixing. A loaded shaft pulls it back, and above 5 RPS the starter asks for nothing.

findings.label: Speed step at 10 RPS, full throttle
findings.value: submitted 10.989 RPS; local step 0.989 RPS per update; weighted step 9.89 (small)
findings.detail: Undamaged, u = 1, r = 10: r_submit = 0.99 × (10 + 0.1 × 11) = 10.989. findings.label: Throttle above which an unloaded engine keeps speeding up
findings.detail: Above 2 RPS the step 0.99 × (r + 0.1 × u × (r + 1)) - r = 0.099 × u × (r + 1) - 0.01 × r is positive at every r when u ≥ 0.01 ÷ 0.099 = 0.101. With no other shaft member the group speed follows the engine's own step, so above that throttle an unloaded engine accelerates until the RPS Limiter cuts the throttle. A calculation from the recovered constants, not a game measurement. Report: investigation/classic-engines.md. findings.detail: Diesel L/s = 60 × 10 L × 0.00002 × s × u × r × g(r) = 0.012 × s × u × r × g(r), with u = 1 and enough diesel and air. limitations: The classic update 0x14034ba00 was decoded by static analysis of one build; the game was not run. A conversion of the shaft weight and speed steps to SI torque in N m, watts or joules was not recovered.

Engine temperature depends on RPS history, coolant flow and the surrounding-temperature sample, so no single temperature per throttle setting exists. The weather part of that sample depends on texture values at the engine's position; the Weather temperature, lighting and hazards mechanics article lists what of it remains open.

Non-finite speeds are decoded only for the speed branch: it does not sanitize NaN or infinity. The complete non-finite fluid and network behaviour was not traced. Thermal efficiency in physical units is unknown.

For active, normally simulated vehicles, these formulas run once per nominal 1/60-second simulation update. Multiply per-update amounts by 60 for amounts per simulated second. A constant relaxation fraction k leaves (1-k)^60 of a gap after one simulated second. Physics solver substeps and render frames are separate; pauses, sleeping, unloaded vehicles and real-time slowdown are outside this conversion.

families.summary: Air fans on the shared force-emitter law with pitch fixed at 1; at 10 RPS they give 145.979 or 254.764 and 225.830 or 432.141 internal force per RPS depending on the air weight branch, before the application cap.

sections.title: Thrust and shaft load
sections.body:
Each update the part reads its published shaft speed and computes w = RPS × 0.9999, the effective pitch p = clamp(saved pitch + input, -1, 1) and the load b = (2 × w × rotation_speed × π × blade_physics_length × p × 0.75 + p × U) × blade_efficiency × B × 0.32, where U is the relative flow along the thrust axis and B the number of intact blades. With q = clamp(b × 0.5 ÷ K, -10, 10), multiplied by 10 when the hub is below the water surface, it removes w × (1 - 1 ÷ (1 + q²)) RPS from its own speed and pushes with T = 1500 × K × removed RPS × efficiency, signed by the pitch.

The fans have only an RPS port, so the effective pitch stays at force_emitter_default_pitch 1. Turning the shaft backwards reverses the push.

sections.title: Sizes
sections.body:
Small Ducted Fan: K 2 or 1, 145.979 or 254.764 per RPS; Large Ducted Fan: K 10 or 5, 225.830 or 432.141 per RPS. Figures are raw internal force per input RPS at 10 published RPS, effective pitch 1, 4 intact blades and no inflow, before the application cap.

Air parts take one of two solver weights, K = F ÷ 1000 or F × B ÷ 8000, depending on a definition byte the decode could not tie to a resource field; each figure gives both, the first for F ÷ 1000. Their small F gives a small K, so they take more speed off the shaft per RPS than the rotors.

sections.title: Water and altitude
sections.body: With the hub below the water surface a fan pushes not at all, and its load ratio is multiplied by 10. Thrust is multiplied by (1 - 2.2413793e-5 × y)^5.3595023 of the vehicle's altitude y: 1 at sea level, 0 above 40000.

For active, normally simulated vehicles, these formulas run once per nominal 1/60-second simulation update. Multiply per-update amounts by 60 for amounts per simulated second. Physics solver substeps and render frames are separate; pauses, sleeping, unloaded vehicles and real-time slowdown are outside this conversion.

families.summary: Capacity is electric_charge_capacity (1600, 12800, 256000). Each update a battery lends at most 10 × its charge fraction to the network pool, so more batteries supply more per update while a bigger battery lasts longer.

sections.title: Variant tradeoffs
sections.body: The medium battery stores 8 times and the large 160 times the small battery's charge. All three lend the same packet of at most 10 per update, 600 per simulated second when full.

sections.title: Charge and discharge
sections.body:
A lone battery with nothing else on the network can give at most 10 × b per update, where b is its fraction, so a load that takes everything leaves b × (1 − 10 ÷ C) after each update. After one simulated second of that the small, medium and large battery keep 0.686, 0.954 and 0.998 of their charge. With N equally charged batteries, no generation and no other load, a request R gets q × min(1, 10 × N ÷ R) of what it asks.

Charging has no cap of its own. A deposit Q into a lone battery's pool raises its fraction by Q ÷ C up to full, and the surplus is lost. An idle lone battery loses nothing, because the loan and the return cancel. Batteries sharing a network move toward the pool fraction q by 10 × (q − b) ÷ C per update, so a small battery evens out faster than a large one.

sections.title: Setup and interactions
sections.body: Set Charge Level (0 to 100) in the properties to spawn partially charged. Charge outputs the stored fraction from 0 to 1. The game computes it as clamp(b ÷ ((C − 10) ÷ C), 0, 1) from the fraction left after the pool loan, which for a lone battery is the fraction before the update. While a battery is damaged the update sets its stored fraction, capacity and Charge to 0, so its charge is lost.

families.summary: Pushes fluid with a bias of electrical supply × pump_pressure × Max Power; at equal pressure the small pump moves at most 200 L/s and the large one 400 L/s.

sections.title: Operating conditions
sections.body: The pump needs power and the On/Off signal. Each update it calls the two-port solver with bias = electrical supply × pump_pressure × Max Power. Supply is the share of its electricity request it receives, 1 with unlimited electricity, and Max Power defaults to 100 %. The pump is one-way: it never pushes fluid backward. It holds no fluid itself; its ports connect straight to the pipe networks. Off or damaged, it passes nothing. It requests 0.001 × Max Power electricity per update, the same for both sizes.

sections.title: Flow
sections.body:
At equal pressure on both sides the move is at most min(bias, 20) ÷ 30 amount per update. That is 200 L/s for the small pump and 400 L/s for the large one at full power. The large pump's bias reaches 20 at 20 % Max Power, so it keeps the 400 L/s bound down to that setting. The small pump reaches 200 L/s only at full power, though pressure from upstream can push more through it.

These are bounds. Real flow falls with fill, backpressure and other ports on the same network. In the report's reference loop with one 3x3 radiator, the small pump settled at 42.6 L/s and the large one at 165.5 L/s. The cooling capacity calculator's finite-flow mode steps such loops.

sections.title: Variant tradeoffs
sections.body: pump_pressure 100 against 10 gives the large pump a tenfold bias, but the solver caps any bias above 20, so at full power its bound is twice the small pump's, not ten times.

sections.title: Open measurement questions
sections.body: Compare Flow Rate in game with the bounds above and with the finite-flow estimate for the same loop.

families.summary: Cools its fluid toward the surrounding temperature at 0.003 × (1 + fan) per update; the electric fan can triple the passive rate.

sections.title: Operating conditions
sections.body: Cooling runs only while both Fluid A and Fluid B are connected. The fan term is 2 × the electrical availability while Fan On/Off is on and power is present; each powered update also draws 0.001 units through the shared electricity helper, 0.06 units per simulated second. Temperature reports the stored water temperature in °C after the cooling step.

sections.title: Performance drivers
sections.body: Cooling multiplier = 1 + fan, with fan clamped to 0…2, so a fully powered fan gives three times the passive rate. Mounted outside an enclosed compartment, airflow counts as fan as speed ÷ 40, with speed in m/s relative to the wind, so at 80 m/s a vehicle reaches full cooling without power. The term alone leaves 0.835 of the gap to ambient after one simulated second at multiplier 1 and 0.581 at multiplier 3.

sections.title: Variant tradeoffs
sections.body: Both sizes run the same rule and fraction. The compartment volume equals the listed voxels: 9 for the 3x3 and 25 for the 5x5, at 10 L per unit. The larger radiator therefore cools more stored water per update, if the pump keeps it filled.

sections.title: Flow through the radiator
sections.body:
Each update the radiator exchanges with its Fluid A network, then its Fluid B network, then cools. Arriving water is mixed by the radiator's amount after the move, and below 0.01 amount per update a direct exchange also moves temperature through the ports. Its volume is capacity: in a pumped loop it need not stay full, and its water settles cooler than the coolant manifold.

For one radiator fed at a fixed inlet temperature with flow q and stored water A, the outlet sits q ÷ (k × A + (1 + k) × q) of the way from ambient to the inlet, with k = 0.003 × (1 + fan). With 9 units of water, 200 L/s and a full fan that is 83.90 °C out for 100 °C in at 20 °C ambient, a 16.10 °C drop. The cooling capacity calculator's finite-flow mode steps whole loops.

sections.title: Surrounding temperature
sections.body: The radiator cools toward the same surrounding temperature the heat exchangers use. It samples it at its own position every 16 updates and ramps to each new sample over 16 updates. Outside a compartment the sample blends the air and water weather temperatures by depth; inside an enclosed compartment it is the compartment's temperature. Nearby heat sources raise it. The weather temperature follows the region, season, time of day, rain and height; the Heat exchange category summarizes it and the Weather temperature, lighting and hazards mechanics article gives the equations.
