limitations: Far-plane figures assume the saved radar_fov default 0.1 and a target on the sensor's axis. S is read per physics body. Mass accounting, the height sampler, blocking materials and other saved radar_fov values are open questions listed under Other components.

families.summary: Legacy sonar: a target passes when its physics-body mass S over distance exceeds 0.25 (d < 4 × S), up to a far plane about 2325 m ahead at the default saved FOV. FOV input 0.01 to 0.125 turns.

sections.title: Detection
sections.body:
Logic case 50 scores each candidate as S ÷ d, with S the target's physics-body mass and d the straight-line distance, and requires more than 0.25, so d < 4 × S. radar_range does not enter the score. It sets the far plane C = P × (0.75 + 0.25 × 0.01 ÷ saved radar_fov) instead: with P = 3000 and the saved default 0.1, C is about 2325 m.

On the sensor's axis a target passes within min(2325, 4 × S) m: 40 m for S = 10, 400 m for S = 100, 2325 m for S = 1000. Off the axis the straight-line distance can exceed C. The target must also lie inside four side planes set by the FOV. Candidates go best score first through a line-of-sight query, and the first that passes is output.

sections.title: Field of view and aim
sections.body: The FOV input is clamped to 0.01 to 0.125 turn, 3.6 to 45 degrees horizontally; the vertical field is fixed at 0.25 turn, 90 degrees. Facing Yaw is clamped to -0.5 to 0.5 turn. Changing the FOV moves the side planes only: the far plane follows the saved radar_fov field, default 0.1.

sections.title: Water and height gates
sections.body: The sonar runs only while its position is at least 0.25 m below a sampled height, and it sees only targets whose lowest point is below y = -1. Reading that height as the water surface is an inference. It does not use the advanced sonar's ping, passive listening or echo timing.

sections.title: Setup and interactions
sections.body: Outputs give distance in metres and angles in turns. They carry no SDK noise: radar_noise, radar_distance_noise and sonar_noise do not reach this logic case.

limitations: Far-plane figures assume the saved radar_fov default 0.1 and a target on the sensor's axis. S is read per physics body. Mass accounting, the height sampler, blocking materials and other saved radar_fov values are open questions listed under Other components.

families.summary: Legacy sonar: a target passes when its physics-body mass S over distance exceeds 0.25 (d < 4 × S), up to a far plane about 775 m ahead at the default saved FOV. FOV input 0.01 to 0.125 turns.

sections.title: Detection
sections.body:
Logic case 50 scores each candidate as S ÷ d, with S the target's physics-body mass and d the straight-line distance, and requires more than 0.25, so d < 4 × S. radar_range does not enter the score. It sets the far plane C = P × (0.75 + 0.25 × 0.01 ÷ saved radar_fov) instead: with P = 1000 and the saved default 0.1, C is about 775 m.

On the sensor's axis a target passes within min(775, 4 × S) m: 40 m for S = 10, 400 m for S = 100, 775 m for S = 1000. Off the axis the straight-line distance can exceed C. The target must also lie inside four side planes set by the FOV. Candidates go best score first through a line-of-sight query, and the first that passes is output.

sections.title: Field of view and aim
sections.body: The FOV input is clamped to 0.01 to 0.125 turn, 3.6 to 45 degrees horizontally; the vertical field is fixed at 0.25 turn, 90 degrees. Facing Yaw is clamped to -0.5 to 0.5 turn. Changing the FOV moves the side planes only: the far plane follows the saved radar_fov field, default 0.1.

sections.title: Water and height gates
sections.body: The sonar runs only while its position is at least 0.25 m below a sampled height, and it sees only targets whose lowest point is below y = -1. Reading that height as the water surface is an inference. It does not use the advanced sonar's ping, passive listening or echo timing.

sections.title: Setup and interactions
sections.body: Outputs give distance in metres and angles in turns. They carry no SDK noise: radar_noise, radar_distance_noise and sonar_noise do not reach this logic case.

limitations: Far-plane figures assume the saved radar_fov default 0.1 and a target on the sensor's axis. S is read per physics body. Mass accounting, the height sampler, blocking materials and other saved radar_fov values are open questions listed under Other components.

families.summary: Outputs the sum of live sources within reach, s × (1 − d ÷ (10 × s)), plus the contamination of the compartment it sits in; outside compartments it adds persistent contamination records instead.

sections.title: Reading
sections.body: Logic case 59 transforms the detector's position to world space, calls the radiation sampler and writes the result unscaled to the Radiation output. A damaged detector outputs 0. Each fuel rod with a reaction above 0.001 is a live source of strength s = 0.1 × r and reach 10 × s metres, reduced by 200 m when it sits in another compartment; sources add with linear falloff. Inside a compartment the detector also adds that compartment's contamination, which fuel assemblies raise by 0.001 × reaction ÷ total amount per update. Outside a compartment it adds persistent contamination records instead, each (1 − d ÷ radius) × amplitude; damaged fuel rods create them with radius 200.

sections.title: Example
sections.body: A fuel rod at the cap r = 50 in the detector's compartment reads 5 at the rod, 2.5 at 25 m and 0 from 50 m. A rod settled at r = 0.18, as in the 2 by 2 example at insertion 0.25, reaches only 0.18 m, so most of a reactor's reading comes from its coolant contamination.

families.summary: Copies Composite Input, On/Off Input, Video Data Send and Audio Data Send to the linked anchor's matching outputs once per update: all 32 on/off and 32 number channels, the video descriptor and a private copy of the audio samples.

sections.title: Setup and interactions
sections.body: Draw one rope logic link to another Electrical Cable Anchor. Wire what one end should send to its Composite Input, On/Off Input, Video Data Send and Audio Data Send, and read it at the other end's Composite Output, On/Off Output, Video Data Receive and Audio Data Receive.

sections.title: How it updates
sections.body: The anchor is a type 48 rope hook with subtype 2. Its signal copy runs in the rope-hook pass (slot +0x360), which the dispatcher calls for each vehicle after every component has updated and before that vehicle's outputs are flushed. With a linked peer and both anchors' internal state below 5, the anchor copies its Composite Input value, all 132 bytes, to the peer's Composite Output, its on/off input to the peer's On/Off Output, its video descriptor to the peer's Video Data Receive and its audio samples to the peer's Audio Data Receive. Each copy replaces the previous one. Nothing is buffered, averaged or scaled, and the 32 + 32 channels arrive unchanged.

sections.title: Video and audio
sections.body: Video is a fixed descriptor copied field by field: no pixels are copied and nothing is allocated. Audio is copied sample by sample into a buffer the receiving anchor owns, reallocated as count × 4 bytes when the sample count changes, so the two ends never share one sample buffer.

sections.title: Electric cable pulleys
sections.body:
Electric Cable Pulleys are rope hooks of subtype 9. When either side of a link is a pulley, the same copies run through the pulley's own buffers, so a cable through a pulley still carries every channel. The on/off value takes the same route through the pulley's own on/off bytes.

Each end stores its peer per side: a connection named Rope 2 uses the second link slot and any other the first, so the two ends of one link can use different slots. A pulley hands what one side receives straight to the peer on its other side in the same pass, with no delay of its own. A value therefore crosses several pulleys in one pass when they are processed in route order, and each hop whose next pulley is processed earlier adds a pass: passes = 1 + the number of such reversals. That order depends on the vehicle, so a cable route has no fixed delay per pulley.

families.summary: Links the fluid networks at both ends of a hose with bias 0, both directions and exchange factor 0.5; hose length adds no volume or resistance.

sections.title: Operating conditions
sections.body: A rope logic link between two anchors forms the hose. Each update the end that holds the link's exchange flag calls the two-port solver between the Fluid Node networks at the two ends with bias 0, both directions, all species and factor 0.5, which halves the per-update step limit. When the far end is a hose pulley the link uses the pulley's matching port.

sections.title: Setup and interactions
sections.body: The anchor stores no fluid and the exchange reads no length, so a long hose moves fluid as readily as a short one.

sections.title: Which end exchanges
sections.body: When a hose link between two components is completed, the end that started it gets the exchange flag for that side and the receiving end's flag is cleared, so the link exchanges once per update, from the starting end. A cleared flag on one end does not mean the link is invalid. On hooks with two attachment positions the coupling name Rope 2 selects the second side. A hose end held by a character is a separate link to that character: it clears the component's exchange flag and adds no second hook, so the hook-to-hook exchange does not run for it.

families.summary: Reels 0.48 m/s at Speed 1 (0.048 to 4.8 m/s over the editor range 0.1 to 10) and adds 40 m to the rope's shared length limit.

sections.title: Reel speed
sections.body: Each update a held Down lengthens the rope by b × Speed metres and Up shortens it by the same, with b = 0.0002 × cable_length. For this winch b = 0.008 m, so it reels 0.48 m/s at the default Speed 1. The Speed property runs from 0.1 to 10 in the editor, 0.048 to 4.8 m/s. The Speed input takes a value from -1 to 1. At a magnitude of 0.1 or more it replaces the buttons and moves the rope by b × Speed × that value per update, and negative values shorten the rope. These rates change the rope's rest length. A loaded hook can lag behind it (inference).

sections.title: Length limits
sections.body: Both ends of a rope share one limit, the sum of their cable_length values: 40 m with an anchor at the other end, which adds 0, and more with a second winch. A step is kept only if the new length stays above 0.1 m and below that sum. A step that would cross a bound is dropped, not clamped, so the rope stops up to one step short: a Small Winch at 9.999 m stays at 9.999 m because 10.001 m is not below 10. Two winches on one rope reel at the sum of their rates. If the rope is already longer than the limit, each update shortens it by one step.

sections.title: Both buttons and electricity
sections.body: Holding Up and Down together cancels: the two steps sum to 0, the length does not change and the winch is not flagged as moving. After each accepted step the winch requests 0.01 charge units, 0.6 per simulated second while it keeps reeling, whatever the Speed. The reply does not scale the step. With no usable electricity, from no charge or a full EMP countdown, the buttons are ignored. Static inference: the Speed input still moves the rope in that state, because it bypasses the button gate.

sections.title: Fluid through the cable
sections.body: A rope-hook link moves fluid between the networks on the Fluid ports at its two ends through the two-port solver, with bias 0 in both directions and factor 0.5, or 1 when the exchange runs from a hose pulley. It reads no cable length and adds no hose volume.

limitations: The decoded reel and rope code has no maximum tension or snapping threshold. Rope stiffness and any cap or severing path elsewhere in the solver are listed as open items in the Winch controls, length and hose connections mechanics article.
Static analysis of one build. Reel rates are changes of the rope's rest length; no loaded hook travel was measured in a running game.

For active, normally simulated vehicles, these formulas run once per nominal 1/60-second simulation update. Multiply per-update amounts by 60 for amounts per simulated second. A constant relaxation fraction k leaves (1-k)^60 of a gap after one simulated second. Physics solver substeps and render frames are separate; pauses, sleeping, unloaded vehicles and real-time slowdown are outside this conversion.

families.summary: Reels 7.2 m/s at Speed 1 (0.72 to 72 m/s over the editor range 0.1 to 10) and adds 600 m to the rope's shared length limit.

sections.title: Reel speed
sections.body: Each update a held Down lengthens the rope by b × Speed metres and Up shortens it by the same, with b = 0.0002 × cable_length. For this winch b = 0.12 m, so it reels 7.2 m/s at the default Speed 1. The Speed property runs from 0.1 to 10 in the editor, 0.72 to 72 m/s. The Speed input takes a value from -1 to 1. At a magnitude of 0.1 or more it replaces the buttons and moves the rope by b × Speed × that value per update, and negative values shorten the rope. These rates change the rope's rest length. A loaded hook can lag behind it (inference).

sections.title: Length limits
sections.body: Both ends of a rope share one limit, the sum of their cable_length values: 600 m with an anchor at the other end, which adds 0, and more with a second winch. A step is kept only if the new length stays above 0.1 m and below that sum. A step that would cross a bound is dropped, not clamped, so the rope stops up to one step short: a Small Winch at 9.999 m stays at 9.999 m because 10.001 m is not below 10. Two winches on one rope reel at the sum of their rates. If the rope is already longer than the limit, each update shortens it by one step.

sections.title: Both buttons and electricity
sections.body: Holding Up and Down together cancels: the two steps sum to 0, the length does not change and the winch is not flagged as moving. After each accepted step the winch requests 0.01 charge units, 0.6 per simulated second while it keeps reeling, whatever the Speed. The reply does not scale the step. With no usable electricity, from no charge or a full EMP countdown, the buttons are ignored. Static inference: the Speed input still moves the rope in that state, because it bypasses the button gate.

sections.title: Fluid through the cable
sections.body: A rope-hook link moves fluid between the networks on the Fluid ports at its two ends through the two-port solver, with bias 0 in both directions and factor 0.5, or 1 when the exchange runs from a hose pulley. It reads no cable length and adds no hose volume.

limitations: The decoded reel and rope code has no maximum tension or snapping threshold. Rope stiffness and any cap or severing path elsewhere in the solver are listed as open items in the Winch controls, length and hose connections mechanics article.
Static analysis of one build. Reel rates are changes of the rope's rest length; no loaded hook travel was measured in a running game.

For active, normally simulated vehicles, these formulas run once per nominal 1/60-second simulation update. Multiply per-update amounts by 60 for amounts per simulated second. A constant relaxation fraction k leaves (1-k)^60 of a gap after one simulated second. Physics solver substeps and render frames are separate; pauses, sleeping, unloaded vehicles and real-time slowdown are outside this conversion.

families.summary: Reels 1.8 m/s at Speed 1 (0.18 to 18 m/s over the editor range 0.1 to 10) and adds 150 m to the rope's shared length limit.

sections.title: Reel speed
sections.body: Each update a held Down lengthens the rope by b × Speed metres and Up shortens it by the same, with b = 0.0002 × cable_length. For this winch b = 0.03 m, so it reels 1.8 m/s at the default Speed 1. The Speed property runs from 0.1 to 10 in the editor, 0.18 to 18 m/s. The Speed input takes a value from -1 to 1. At a magnitude of 0.1 or more it replaces the buttons and moves the rope by b × Speed × that value per update, and negative values shorten the rope. These rates change the rope's rest length. A loaded hook can lag behind it (inference).

sections.title: Length limits
sections.body: Both ends of a rope share one limit, the sum of their cable_length values: 150 m with an anchor at the other end, which adds 0, and more with a second winch. A step is kept only if the new length stays above 0.1 m and below that sum. A step that would cross a bound is dropped, not clamped, so the rope stops up to one step short: a Small Winch at 9.999 m stays at 9.999 m because 10.001 m is not below 10. Two winches on one rope reel at the sum of their rates. If the rope is already longer than the limit, each update shortens it by one step.

sections.title: Both buttons and electricity
sections.body: Holding Up and Down together cancels: the two steps sum to 0, the length does not change and the winch is not flagged as moving. After each accepted step the winch requests 0.01 charge units, 0.6 per simulated second while it keeps reeling, whatever the Speed. The reply does not scale the step. With no usable electricity, from no charge or a full EMP countdown, the buttons are ignored. Static inference: the Speed input still moves the rope in that state, because it bypasses the button gate.

sections.title: Fluid through the cable
sections.body: A rope-hook link moves fluid between the networks on the Fluid ports at its two ends through the two-port solver, with bias 0 in both directions and factor 0.5, or 1 when the exchange runs from a hose pulley. It reads no cable length and adds no hose volume.

limitations: The decoded reel and rope code has no maximum tension or snapping threshold. Rope stiffness and any cap or severing path elsewhere in the solver are listed as open items in the Winch controls, length and hose connections mechanics article.
Static analysis of one build. Reel rates are changes of the rope's rest length; no loaded hook travel was measured in a running game.

For active, normally simulated vehicles, these formulas run once per nominal 1/60-second simulation update. Multiply per-update amounts by 60 for amounts per simulated second. A constant relaxation fraction k leaves (1-k)^60 of a gap after one simulated second. Physics solver substeps and render frames are separate; pauses, sleeping, unloaded vehicles and real-time slowdown are outside this conversion.

families.summary: Reels 0.12 m/s at Speed 1 (0.012 to 1.2 m/s over the editor range 0.1 to 10) and adds 10 m to the rope's shared length limit.

sections.title: Reel speed
sections.body: Each update a held Down lengthens the rope by b × Speed metres and Up shortens it by the same, with b = 0.0002 × cable_length. For this winch b = 0.002 m, so it reels 0.12 m/s at the default Speed 1. The Speed property runs from 0.1 to 10 in the editor, 0.012 to 1.2 m/s. These rates change the rope's rest length. A loaded hook can lag behind it (inference).

sections.title: Length limits
sections.body: Both ends of a rope share one limit, the sum of their cable_length values: 10 m with an anchor at the other end, which adds 0, and more with a second winch. A step is kept only if the new length stays above 0.1 m and below that sum. A step that would cross a bound is dropped, not clamped, so the rope stops up to one step short: a Small Winch at 9.999 m stays at 9.999 m because 10.001 m is not below 10. Two winches on one rope reel at the sum of their rates. If the rope is already longer than the limit, each update shortens it by one step.

sections.title: Both buttons and electricity
sections.body: Holding Up and Down together cancels: the two steps sum to 0, the length does not change and the winch is not flagged as moving. After each accepted step the winch requests 0.01 charge units, 0.6 per simulated second while it keeps reeling, whatever the Speed. The reply does not scale the step. With no usable electricity, from no charge or a full EMP countdown, the buttons are ignored.

sections.title: Fluid through the cable
sections.body: A rope-hook link moves fluid between the networks on the Fluid ports at its two ends through the two-port solver, with bias 0 in both directions and factor 0.5, or 1 when the exchange runs from a hose pulley. It reads no cable length and adds no hose volume.

For active, normally simulated vehicles, these formulas run once per nominal 1/60-second simulation update. Multiply per-update amounts by 60 for amounts per simulated second. A constant relaxation fraction k leaves (1-k)^60 of a gap after one simulated second. families.summary: Light end rotor with one power connection on the shared force-emitter law; at 10 RPS it gives 26.603 or 52.979 internal force per RPS by air weight branch, like the light through-drive rotor.

sections.title: Thrust and shaft load
sections.body:
Each update the part reads its published shaft speed and computes w = RPS × 0.9999, the effective pitch p = clamp(saved pitch + input, -1, 1) and the load b = (2 × w × rotation_speed × π × blade_physics_length × p × 0.75 + p × U) × blade_efficiency × B × 0.32, where U is the relative flow along the thrust axis and B the number of intact blades. With q = clamp(b × 0.5 ÷ K, -10, 10), multiplied by 10 when the hub is below the water surface, it removes w × (1 - 1 ÷ (1 + q²)) RPS from its own speed and pushes with T = 1500 × K × removed RPS × efficiency, signed by the pitch.

The saved pitch starts at force_emitter_default_pitch 1, so effective pitch is clamp(1 + Collective): Collective -1 gives zero load and zero thrust, and 0 or more gives full pitch 1. Pitch alone cannot reverse their push; reversing the shaft does.

sections.title: Figures
sections.body:
Rotor End (Light): K 10 or 5, 26.603 or 52.979 per RPS. Figures are raw internal force per input RPS at 10 published RPS, effective pitch 1, 4 intact blades and no inflow, before the application cap.

Air parts take one of two solver weights, K = F ÷ 1000 or F × B ÷ 8000, depending on a definition byte the decode could not tie to a resource field; each figure gives both, the first for F ÷ 1000.

sections.title: End of a stack
sections.body: It has no port B, so the binding installs no A/B link. Because of the coaxial flag the rotor also applies two equal and opposite forces along local X, above and below the hub, each 800 × b × clamp(|saved pitch + Collective + 0.1|, 0, 1). They form a moment about the rotor axis that turns the vehicle against the rotor.

sections.title: Cyclic and hinge
sections.body:
Roll and Pitch, clamped to -1 to 1, move the point where the force acts by -4 × input along local X and Z and tilt the force direction by 0.4 × input. This tips the vehicle; no blade-by-blade phase is modelled.

The rotor body turns on a physical hinge whose motor is on while the RPS port is connected. Its impulse limit is 1000 for every size, and its target speed follows the speed the rotor kept on the previous update × force_emitter_rotation_speed.

sections.title: Water and altitude
sections.body:
With the hub below the water surface the rotor pushes not at all in this update, while its load ratio q is multiplied by 10, so it brakes the shaft much harder. The tooltip's decreased force is this cut-off.

Thrust is multiplied by (1 - 2.2413793e-5 × y)^5.3595023 of the vehicle's altitude y: 1 at sea level, 0 above 40000.

For active, normally simulated vehicles, these formulas run once per nominal 1/60-second simulation update. Multiply per-update amounts by 60 for amounts per simulated second. A constant relaxation fraction k leaves (1-k)^60 of a gap after one simulated second. Physics solver substeps and render frames are separate; pauses, sleeping, unloaded vehicles and real-time slowdown are outside this conversion.

families.summary: Directional link with rx_range 8000000 that needs the Space DLC owned and enabled; must be aimed at the target antenna. By inference its gain falls to 0 about 2.87 degrees off axis.

sections.title: Setup and interactions
sections.body: Steer with Target Yaw and Target Pitch (pitch at most 0.1 turns). Transmit Mode defaults to receive. It carries audio, composite and video.

sections.title: Range and aim
sections.body:
It uses the shared radio receive routine: strength (1 − d ÷ R) × g_r × g_t, with R the sum of both antennas' rx_range at full power and sea level, 16000000 m for two of these. Height, power and submersion change R as for every radio.

Each directional end has its own gain, clamp((v · w − 0.99875) × 800), from its aim direction v and the direction w to the other antenna. Inference, reading v · w as cos θ: the gain is 1 only exactly on axis, 0.5 at 2.03 degrees and 0 from 2.87 degrees. The gain is also 0 unless the Space DLC gate below passes.

sections.title: Space DLC
sections.body:
Each directional end passes its gain through a gate that tests two flags: whether this copy of the game owns the Space DLC, and whether the Space DLC is enabled in the current session. At startup the game asks Steam about the DLC and stores the answer in both. Session setup, joining and server state then set the second flag only when the DLC is owned and the session's DLC mask has its Space value 4, and clear it otherwise. A server cannot enable the DLC for a player who does not own it, and owning it does not enable it in a session that has Space turned off.

Without the Space DLC owned and enabled, directional antenna gain is 0, so the received strength is 0 however well the antenna is aimed. The range figures above assume the gate passes.

families.summary: Directional link with rx_range 10000000 that needs the Space DLC owned and enabled; must be aimed at the target antenna. By inference its gain falls to 0 about 2.87 degrees off axis.

sections.title: Setup and interactions
sections.body: Steer with Target Yaw and Target Pitch (pitch at most 0.1 turns). Transmit Mode defaults to receive. It carries audio, composite and video.

sections.title: Range and aim
sections.body:
It uses the shared radio receive routine: strength (1 − d ÷ R) × g_r × g_t, with R the sum of both antennas' rx_range at full power and sea level, 20000000 m for two of these. Height, power and submersion change R as for every radio.

Each directional end has its own gain, clamp((v · w − 0.99875) × 800), from its aim direction v and the direction w to the other antenna. Inference, reading v · w as cos θ: the gain is 1 only exactly on axis, 0.5 at 2.03 degrees and 0 from 2.87 degrees. The gain is also 0 unless the Space DLC gate below passes.

sections.title: Space DLC
sections.body:
Each directional end passes its gain through a gate that tests two flags: whether this copy of the game owns the Space DLC, and whether the Space DLC is enabled in the current session. At startup the game asks Steam about the DLC and stores the answer in both. Session setup, joining and server state then set the second flag only when the DLC is owned and the session's DLC mask has its Space value 4, and clear it otherwise. A server cannot enable the DLC for a player who does not own it, and owning it does not enable it in a session that has Space turned off.

Without the Space DLC owned and enabled, directional antenna gain is 0, so the received strength is 0 however well the antenna is aimed. The range figures above assume the gate passes.

families.summary: Legacy radio with the same rx_range as its v2 model, 20000 m; two of them at sea level and full power hear each other out to 40000 m, at strength 0.5 at 20000 m.

sections.title: Range and signal strength
sections.body:
Antennas d metres apart in a straight line get strength 1 − d ÷ R, lost at d = R. At full power with both antennas at sea level, R is the sum of both antennas' rx_range. With this antenna's 20000 m that is 20100 m to a Small, 21000 m to a Medium, 24000 m to a Large, 40000 m to a Huge. Strength is 0.5 at half those distances, so two antennas of this size are at 0.5 at the tooltip's 20000 m.

A receiver keeps only the strongest transmitter on its frequency; signals do not add. No terrain, obstacle or weather term takes part.

sections.title: Height, power and water
sections.body: Both antennas' power fractions multiply R: half power at both ends gives 0.25 R. A height bonus adds range only when the receiving antenna is high, above about 5413 m with the transmitter at sea level or above about 3251 m with both at one altitude. For two Small antennas with the receiver at 10000 m and the transmitter at sea level, R is about 15363 m instead of 200 m; the other way round it stays 200 m. Below y = 0 the range shrinks, to 0.25 R when both antennas are submerged.

sections.title: Variant tradeoffs
sections.body: The legacy definition's tooltip states no range, but its rx_range equals the v2 radio's, whose tooltip gives the range, and both run the same receive routine with the same formula. Unlike v2 it has separate send and receive frequencies and no audio, and it has no signal strength port.

families.summary: Range 20000 per tooltip and rx_range field; two of them at sea level hear each other out to 40000 m. Defaults to receive.

sections.title: Range and signal strength
sections.body:
Antennas d metres apart in a straight line get strength 1 − d ÷ R, lost at d = R. At full power with both antennas at sea level, R is the sum of both antennas' rx_range. With this antenna's 20000 m that is 20100 m to a Small, 21000 m to a Medium, 24000 m to a Large, 40000 m to a Huge. Strength is 0.5 at half those distances, so two antennas of this size are at 0.5 at the tooltip's 20000 m.

A receiver keeps only the strongest transmitter on its frequency; signals do not add. No terrain, obstacle or weather term takes part.

sections.title: Height, power and water
sections.body: Both antennas' power fractions multiply R: half power at both ends gives 0.25 R. A height bonus adds range only when the receiving antenna is high, above about 5413 m with the transmitter at sea level or above about 3251 m with both at one altitude. For two Small antennas with the receiver at 10000 m and the transmitter at sea level, R is about 15363 m instead of 200 m; the other way round it stays 200 m. Below y = 0 the range shrinks, to 0.25 R when both antennas are submerged.

sections.title: Setup and interactions
sections.body:
Transmit Mode defaults to receive; set it on to send. One frequency is shared for send and receive. While transmitting, the radio does not receive (inference: the record's transmit byte follows Transmit Mode).

There is no signal strength port. Inference from the receive routine: received audio stays at full level out to half of R and fades to 0 at R, and composite data arrives unscaled whenever the signal is heard.

families.summary: Legacy radio with the same rx_range as its v2 model, 4000 m; two of them at sea level and full power hear each other out to 8000 m, at strength 0.5 at 4000 m.

sections.title: Range and signal strength
sections.body:
Antennas d metres apart in a straight line get strength 1 − d ÷ R, lost at d = R. At full power with both antennas at sea level, R is the sum of both antennas' rx_range. With this antenna's 4000 m that is 4100 m to a Small, 5000 m to a Medium, 8000 m to a Large, 24000 m to a Huge. Strength is 0.5 at half those distances, so two antennas of this size are at 0.5 at the tooltip's 4000 m.

A receiver keeps only the strongest transmitter on its frequency; signals do not add. No terrain, obstacle or weather term takes part.

sections.title: Height, power and water
sections.body: Both antennas' power fractions multiply R: half power at both ends gives 0.25 R. A height bonus adds range only when the receiving antenna is high, above about 5413 m with the transmitter at sea level or above about 3251 m with both at one altitude. For two Small antennas with the receiver at 10000 m and the transmitter at sea level, R is about 15363 m instead of 200 m; the other way round it stays 200 m. Below y = 0 the range shrinks, to 0.25 R when both antennas are submerged.

sections.title: Variant tradeoffs
sections.body: The legacy definition's tooltip states no range, but its rx_range equals the v2 radio's, whose tooltip gives the range, and both run the same receive routine with the same formula. Unlike v2 it has separate send and receive frequencies and no audio, and it has no signal strength port.

families.summary: Range 4000 per tooltip and rx_range field; two of them at sea level hear each other out to 8000 m. Defaults to receive.

sections.title: Range and signal strength
sections.body:
Antennas d metres apart in a straight line get strength 1 − d ÷ R, lost at d = R. At full power with both antennas at sea level, R is the sum of both antennas' rx_range. With this antenna's 4000 m that is 4100 m to a Small, 5000 m to a Medium, 8000 m to a Large, 24000 m to a Huge. Strength is 0.5 at half those distances, so two antennas of this size are at 0.5 at the tooltip's 4000 m.

A receiver keeps only the strongest transmitter on its frequency; signals do not add. No terrain, obstacle or weather term takes part.

sections.title: Height, power and water
sections.body: Both antennas' power fractions multiply R: half power at both ends gives 0.25 R. A height bonus adds range only when the receiving antenna is high, above about 5413 m with the transmitter at sea level or above about 3251 m with both at one altitude. For two Small antennas with the receiver at 10000 m and the transmitter at sea level, R is about 15363 m instead of 200 m; the other way round it stays 200 m. Below y = 0 the range shrinks, to 0.25 R when both antennas are submerged.

sections.title: Setup and interactions
sections.body:
Transmit Mode defaults to receive; set it on to send. One frequency is shared for send and receive. While transmitting, the radio does not receive (inference: the record's transmit byte follows Transmit Mode).

There is no signal strength port. Inference from the receive routine: received audio stays at full level out to half of R and fades to 0 at R, and composite data arrives unscaled whenever the signal is heard.

families.summary: Legacy radio with the same rx_range as its v2 model, 1000 m; two of them at sea level and full power hear each other out to 2000 m, at strength 0.5 at 1000 m.

sections.title: Range and signal strength
sections.body:
Antennas d metres apart in a straight line get strength 1 − d ÷ R, lost at d = R. At full power with both antennas at sea level, R is the sum of both antennas' rx_range. With this antenna's 1000 m that is 1100 m to a Small, 2000 m to a Medium, 5000 m to a Large, 21000 m to a Huge. Strength is 0.5 at half those distances, so two antennas of this size are at 0.5 at the tooltip's 1000 m.

A receiver keeps only the strongest transmitter on its frequency; signals do not add. No terrain, obstacle or weather term takes part.

sections.title: Height, power and water
sections.body: Both antennas' power fractions multiply R: half power at both ends gives 0.25 R. A height bonus adds range only when the receiving antenna is high, above about 5413 m with the transmitter at sea level or above about 3251 m with both at one altitude. For two Small antennas with the receiver at 10000 m and the transmitter at sea level, R is about 15363 m instead of 200 m; the other way round it stays 200 m. Below y = 0 the range shrinks, to 0.25 R when both antennas are submerged.

sections.title: Variant tradeoffs
sections.body: The legacy definition's tooltip states no range, but its rx_range equals the v2 radio's, whose tooltip gives the range, and both run the same receive routine with the same formula. Unlike v2 it has separate send and receive frequencies and no audio, and it has no signal strength port.

findings.label: Sea-level radio reach
findings.value: R = rx_range of receiver + rx_range of transmitter
findings.detail: At full power with both antennas at y = 0, H = 0 and q = 0, so R is the sum of both rx_range values and strength is 0.5 at half that distance. Ordinary rx_range: Small 100 m, Medium 1000 m, Large 4000 m, Huge 20000 m. families.summary: Range 1000 per tooltip and rx_range field; two of them at sea level hear each other out to 2000 m. Defaults to receive.

sections.title: Range and signal strength
sections.body:
Antennas d metres apart in a straight line get strength 1 − d ÷ R, lost at d = R. At full power with both antennas at sea level, R is the sum of both antennas' rx_range. With this antenna's 1000 m that is 1100 m to a Small, 2000 m to a Medium, 5000 m to a Large, 21000 m to a Huge. Strength is 0.5 at half those distances, so two antennas of this size are at 0.5 at the tooltip's 1000 m.

A receiver keeps only the strongest transmitter on its frequency; signals do not add. No terrain, obstacle or weather term takes part.

sections.title: Height, power and water
sections.body: Both antennas' power fractions multiply R: half power at both ends gives 0.25 R. A height bonus adds range only when the receiving antenna is high, above about 5413 m with the transmitter at sea level or above about 3251 m with both at one altitude. For two Small antennas with the receiver at 10000 m and the transmitter at sea level, R is about 15363 m instead of 200 m; the other way round it stays 200 m. Below y = 0 the range shrinks, to 0.25 R when both antennas are submerged.

sections.title: Setup and interactions
sections.body:
Transmit Mode defaults to receive; set it on to send. One frequency is shared for send and receive. While transmitting, the radio does not receive (inference: the record's transmit byte follows Transmit Mode).

There is no signal strength port. Inference from the receive routine: received audio stays at full level out to half of R and fades to 0 at R, and composite data arrives unscaled whenever the signal is heard.

families.summary: Legacy radio with the same rx_range as its v2 model, 100 m; two of them at sea level and full power hear each other out to 200 m, at strength 0.5 at 100 m.

sections.title: Range and signal strength
sections.body:
Antennas d metres apart in a straight line get strength 1 − d ÷ R, lost at d = R. At full power with both antennas at sea level, R is the sum of both antennas' rx_range. With this antenna's 100 m that is 200 m to a Small, 1100 m to a Medium, 4100 m to a Large, 20100 m to a Huge. Strength is 0.5 at half those distances, so two antennas of this size are at 0.5 at the tooltip's 100 m.

A receiver keeps only the strongest transmitter on its frequency; signals do not add. No terrain, obstacle or weather term takes part.

sections.title: Height, power and water
sections.body: Both antennas' power fractions multiply R: half power at both ends gives 0.25 R. A height bonus adds range only when the receiving antenna is high, above about 5413 m with the transmitter at sea level or above about 3251 m with both at one altitude. For two Small antennas with the receiver at 10000 m and the transmitter at sea level, R is about 15363 m instead of 200 m; the other way round it stays 200 m. Below y = 0 the range shrinks, to 0.25 R when both antennas are submerged.

sections.title: Variant tradeoffs
sections.body: The legacy definition's tooltip states no range, but its rx_range equals the v2 radio's, whose tooltip gives the range, and both run the same receive routine with the same formula. Unlike v2 it has separate send and receive frequencies and no audio, and it has no signal strength port.

families.summary: Range 100 per tooltip and rx_range field; two of them at sea level hear each other out to 200 m. Defaults to receive.

sections.title: Range and signal strength
sections.body:
Antennas d metres apart in a straight line get strength 1 − d ÷ R, lost at d = R. At full power with both antennas at sea level, R is the sum of both antennas' rx_range. With this antenna's 100 m that is 200 m to a Small, 1100 m to a Medium, 4100 m to a Large, 20100 m to a Huge. Strength is 0.5 at half those distances, so two antennas of this size are at 0.5 at the tooltip's 100 m.

A receiver keeps only the strongest transmitter on its frequency; signals do not add. No terrain, obstacle or weather term takes part.

sections.title: Height, power and water
sections.body: Both antennas' power fractions multiply R: half power at both ends gives 0.25 R. A height bonus adds range only when the receiving antenna is high, above about 5413 m with the transmitter at sea level or above about 3251 m with both at one altitude. For two Small antennas with the receiver at 10000 m and the transmitter at sea level, R is about 15363 m instead of 200 m; the other way round it stays 200 m. Below y = 0 the range shrinks, to 0.25 R when both antennas are submerged.

sections.title: Setup and interactions
sections.body:
Transmit Mode defaults to receive; set it on to send. One frequency is shared for send and receive. While transmitting, the radio does not receive (inference: the record's transmit byte follows Transmit Mode).

There is no signal strength port. Inference from the receive routine: received audio stays at full level out to half of R and fades to 0 at R, and composite data arrives unscaled whenever the signal is heard.

families.summary: Video receiver with rx_range 10000; its Signal Strength output reads 1 − d ÷ 20000 from a video transmitter d metres away at sea level.

sections.title: Range and signal strength
sections.body: It uses the shared radio receive routine and keeps the strongest video transmitter on its frequency. Signal Strength is (1 − d ÷ R) with R the sum of both rx_range values, 20000 m at full power and sea level, and 0 when nothing is heard. Height, power and submersion change R as for every radio. Inference from the receive routine: the video level is full out to half of R and fades to 0 at R.

families.summary: Takes outside air through its Fluid port. Airspeed in m/s along the part's local +X axis, the side the mouth faces, adds 0.1 × speed of bias, which acts like 2 × that much extra outside pressure; inside an enclosed compartment it is a plain port.

sections.title: Operating conditions
sections.body: Case 0xf shares the fluid-update block of cases 0, 0xc and 0x17, which does nothing until the Fluid port is connected. Each update 0x140311f20 builds the state outside the port. If the scoop sits in an enclosed compartment, outside means that compartment's air, the factor is 1 and no speed term is added. Otherwise the outside is fresh air when the port is above the water surface and sea water when it is below.

sections.title: Outside pressure
sections.body:
Air pressure is (1 - 2.2413793e-05 × y)^5.3595023 with y the port's world height in metres, 1 at sea level, 0.8856 at 1000 m, 0.5289 at 5000 m and 0.2566 at 10000 m. Above 40000 m it is 0. The air is 20 units split 15.792, 4.2 and 0.007999999 across fluid indices 11, 10 and 4, the dry-air nitrogen, oxygen and carbon dioxide shares, though the code does not name them.

Under water the pressure is 30 - 29 ÷ (1 + 0.001 × depth): 1.2871 at 10 m, 3.6364 at 100 m, 15.5 at 1000 m. The outside fluid is 20 units of index 6 plus any oil the world map holds at that spot, so a submerged scoop pulls water.

sections.title: Speed term
sections.body:
The update takes the port's velocity, including spin, subtracts the wind and projects the result on the part's local X axis. The mesh mouth faces local +X, so driving mouth first in still air gives a positive speed; air entering the mouth moves along -X. Speed is in m/s: the linear speed sensor, whose output is documented in m/s, uses the same velocity calculation without conversion.

Bias = 0.1 × voxel count × that speed, clamped to -10…10; the scoop has 1 voxel, so the clamp is hit at 100 m/s. Moving tail first gives a negative bias that favors outflow from the network, and sideways motion adds nothing.

sections.title: Wind
sections.body: The subtracted vector is the vehicle's cached weather wind, so the scoop responds to airspeed rather than ground speed. Facing into a headwind raises the bias, and a tailwind as fast as the vehicle cancels it. The game samples the wind once per vehicle at its transformed origin, not at each scoop. The sample includes local weather-cell wind and is scaled by 1 - shelter, so inside a weather shelter volume it is 0. A vehicle whose parent-body link (vehicle+0x14b8) is set gets zero wind on this path.

sections.title: Flow per update and per second
sections.body:
The port routine works in pressure units where 1 is sea-level air. For a gas-filled pipe network of 8 or more volume units, away from the target-pressure and free-window clamps, the demand is (P_net - (p_out + 2 × bias)) ÷ 15 amount per update, negative meaning inflow, and inflow demand stops growing at 2 ÷ 15 × p_out. The move magnitude is at most 0.5 × factor × the absolute demand, using the network's allocation from the previous update. At exactly P_net - p_out - bias = 0 the routine instead sets demand to 0.

At sea level with the network at pressure 1, a sole scoop moves 0.0167, 0.0333, 0.05 and 0.0667 amount per update at 2.5, 5, 7.5 and 10 m/s, and stays at 0.0667 above that. The port counter stores 600 × the gas amount moved in one update (10, 20, 30 and 40), and the inspection tooltip multiplies it by 60 and shows L/s: 600, 1200, 1800 and 2400 L/s. A stationary scoop on a network an engine has pulled to 0 moves 0.0333 amount per update, 1200 L/s, so speed can double the best static intake. At altitude the maximum inflow scales with p_out while the bias does not. Unsaturated flow does not generally scale in the same way; it depends on network pressure too.

Component updates run 60 times per simulated second, so under the same assumptions the sea-level cap is 4 amount per second, shown as 2400 L/s. The still scoop into a network at 0 takes 2 amount per second (1200 L/s), and below the cap flow into a network at 1 is 0.4 × speed amount per second, 240 × speed L/s up to 10 m/s. The tooltip therefore counts 1 gas amount as 600 L. That factor is fixed and does not divide by network pressure, so the figure is not the compressed volume in the pipes. These are rates at a fixed state; a filling network raises P_net and the flow falls.

sections.title: Near volcanoes
sections.body: In air, the move is also scaled by an exchange factor. Volcanoes lower it: each active volcano adds a source with strength volcanic_heat² and radius 0.5 × eruption_radius at its position. The factor is max(0.01, 1 - volcanic_heat² × eruption_radius ÷ (2 × distance)) for the strongest source, so a hot volcano with a wide eruption radius can cut intake to 0.01 of normal near it. Away from volcanoes the factor is 1. Under water it stays 1.

sections.title: Sealed network
sections.body: The simplified demand has a zero at P_net = p_out + 2 × bias: 3 at 10 m/s, 11 at 50 and 21 at 100 or more, where the bias clamp caps it. The exact branch also gives zero demand at P_net = p_out + bias. These are mathematical zero-demand points, not a verified final pressure for a filling network.

A ray along X through y = 0.0625, z = 0 meets triangles only at x = 0.085 (recess) and x = -0.125 (closed back), none at the x = 0.125 face, so that face is open. Mesh positions are copied unchanged into the vertex buffer and drawn through the component transform times the definition mesh matrix, so mesh +X is component local +X. Report: investigation/air-scoop-followup.md.

findings.label: Scoop speed unit
findings.detail: The scoop's point velocity uses the body fields and helpers of the linear speed sensor, whose output port reads them unscaled and is described as m/s; the scoop subtracts the cached wind before projecting. The angular velocity is then rad/s by dimensional inference. findings.label: Subtracted vector
findings.detail: The vector the scoop and the case 9 radiators subtract is the vehicle's cached weather wind, sampled once per vehicle at its transformed origin and scaled by 1 - shelter; it is zero when vehicle+0x14b8 holds a parent-body link. The scoop therefore responds to airspeed relative to the wind. limitations: Static decompilation of one build; the game was not run and no flow was measured.

For active, normally simulated vehicles, these formulas run once per nominal 1/60-second simulation update. Multiply per-update amounts by 60 for amounts per simulated second. A constant relaxation fraction k leaves (1-k)^60 of a gap after one simulated second. Physics solver substeps and render frames are separate; pauses, sleeping, unloaded vehicles and real-time slowdown are outside this conversion.

The flow figures assume the scoop is the only port moving gas into a network of at least 8 volume units with room to spare. With several ports, the allocation gives each f·|f| ÷ Σ|f|, and the move lags the demand by one update.
Volcanoes are the producer of exchange-factor sources found in this build. The search identified that writer but did not exhaustively exclude every other writer to the list.
The L/s figure on the inspection tooltip is a fixed display factor of 600 L per gas amount. It does not measure the compressed gas volume in the network.

families.summary: Passive and active sonar; tooltip range and radar_range both 60000. Active returns pass out to 600 × S m, and one standard ping is heard within 28200 m.

sections.title: Operating conditions
sections.body: Passively it hears noisy components such as propellers and engines. Holding Ping suppresses passive returns; each new ping overrides the previous one, and active returns appear briefly as the echo arrives.

sections.title: Setup and interactions
sections.body: The sonar data composite carries up to 16 targets as pivot and pitch pairs. Sonar jammers create passive decoys.

sections.title: Detection
sections.body:
With P = radar_range = 60000, an active return at distance d passes when d ≤ P and P ÷ 10000 × S ÷ d > 0.01, that is d < 600 × S m. Returns appear as the echo window passes them, 12.333333 m of distance per update or 740 m per second.

While it is not pinging, it scores another sonar's ping of amplitude 235 as 235 × P × 0.00002 ÷ d against the same 0.01, so one ping is heard within 28200 m, the small advanced sonar's figure. Directions closer than 0.01 in squared difference merge, and each reported angle carries up to ±0.001 turn of noise at the SDK default, spread evenly over 32768 steps.

findings.label: Sonar (Small) · tooltip
findings.value: This sensor outputs the relative angle to detected objects within its range using underwater sound waves. The sensor will passively detect certain noisy components such as propellers or engines but can also send out a loud ping to detect quiet underwater bodies. While the ping input is held passive signals will be supressed. After activating a ping additional detected signals will appear momentarily in the data channel as the signal returns to the sonar. Activating another ping will override the previous ping and no further data will be returned from the old signal.

findings.label: Sensor noise distribution
findings.value: 32768 equally spaced values from −1 to 1, uniform over a full cycle
findings.detail: The advanced sensors form U = result ÷ 32767 and use 2U − 1, so the noise variable takes 32768 equally spaced values including −1 and 1. Inference: the generator has full period 2^32 (odd increment, multiplier 1 modulo 4), so over one cycle each 15-bit output occurs 2^17 times. families.summary: Passive and active sonar; tooltip range and radar_range both 100000. Active returns pass out to 1000 × S m, and one standard ping is heard within 47000 m.

sections.title: Operating conditions
sections.body: Passively it hears noisy components such as propellers and engines. Holding Ping suppresses passive returns; each new ping overrides the previous one, and active returns appear briefly as the echo arrives.

sections.title: Setup and interactions
sections.body: The sonar data composite carries up to 16 targets as pivot and pitch pairs. Sonar jammers create passive decoys.

sections.title: Detection
sections.body:
With P = radar_range = 100000, an active return at distance d passes when d ≤ P and P ÷ 10000 × S ÷ d > 0.01, that is d < 1000 × S m. Returns appear as the echo window passes them, 12.333333 m of distance per update or 740 m per second.

While it is not pinging, it scores another sonar's ping of amplitude 235 as 235 × P × 0.00002 ÷ d against the same 0.01, so one ping is heard within 47000 m, the medium advanced sonar's figure. Directions closer than 0.01 in squared difference merge, and each reported angle carries up to ±0.001 turn of noise at the SDK default, spread evenly over 32768 steps.

findings.label: Sonar (Medium) · tooltip
findings.value: This sensor outputs the relative angle to detected objects within its range using underwater sound waves. The sensor will passively detect certain noisy components such as propellers or engines but can also send out a loud ping to detect quiet underwater bodies. While the ping input is held passive signals will be supressed. After activating a ping additional detected signals will appear momentarily in the data channel as the signal returns to the sonar. Activating another ping will override the previous ping and no further data will be returned from the old signal.

families.summary: Boils water at or above a fixed temperature of 100 at min(0.001 × (T - 100), water) per update, 1:1 by amount, and pushes steam out through Steam Out.

sections.title: Boiling
sections.body: The boiler and condenser convert between water and steam in their phase chamber at a fixed temperature of 100, whatever the pressure. At or above 100, min(0.001 × (T - 100), water) of fresh and salt water becomes steam per update, 1:1 by stored amount, which is 0.06 × (T - 100) per simulated second until water runs short. Below 100, min(0.001 × (100 - T), 0.1 × steam) condenses into fresh water. Each step shifts the chamber temperature by only 0.01 × converted ÷ total amount, so boiling takes almost no heat from the water.

sections.title: Heat transfer
sections.body: Each update the phase and coolant chambers exchange heat with k = 0.1 × (1 - D), D = clamp(0.1 × damage, 0, 1), each side moving by k times the other side's share of the liquid amount. Both chambers then lose 0.0001 of their gap to the surroundings per update. The phase chamber holds 0.1 × voxels, 17.5 here, and the coolant chamber 1 per voxel, 175.

sections.title: Ports
sections.body: Coolant A and B exchange only when both are connected, with no enforced direction and flow scaled by 1 - D. Water In admits fresh water only, one way in, demanding as if the pipe pressure were 60 higher. Steam Out passes steam only, one way out, with a bias of 2.5 × steam ÷ phase volume, so it pushes harder as steam builds up. Salt water already in the chamber still boils.

sections.title: Damage
sections.body: A damaged boiler loses 0.1 × D of its steam per update. No pressure limit or burst test appears in its update.

limitations: Open items for the whole steam cycle are listed under Steam on the parts index.
Static analysis of one build. Temperatures, pressures, amounts and speeds are the game's internal values; no figure here was measured in a running game.

For active, normally simulated vehicles, these formulas run once per nominal 1/60-second simulation update. Multiply per-update amounts by 60 for amounts per simulated second. A constant relaxation fraction k leaves (1-k)^60 of a gap after one simulated second. Physics solver substeps and render frames are separate; pauses, sleeping, unloaded vehicles and real-time slowdown are outside this conversion.

families.summary: Condenses steam below a fixed temperature of 100 at min(0.001 × (100 - T), 0.1 × steam) per update into fresh water; its coolant must keep it below 100.

sections.title: Condensing
sections.body: Below 100 the phase chamber turns min(0.001 × (100 - T), 0.1 × steam) of steam into fresh water per update, at most 10% of the steam. At or above 100 it boils water like a boiler instead. Each step shifts the chamber temperature by only 0.01 × converted ÷ total amount.

sections.title: Heat transfer
sections.body: Each update the phase and coolant chambers exchange heat with k = 0.1 × (1 - D), D = clamp(0.1 × damage, 0, 1), each side moving by k times the other side's share of the liquid amount. The condenser counts its whole phase chamber, steam included. Both chambers then lose 0.0001 of their gap to the surroundings per update. The phase chamber holds 0.1 × voxels, 7.5 here, and the coolant chamber 1 per voxel, 75.

sections.title: Ports
sections.body: Coolant A and B exchange only when both are connected, with no enforced direction. Steam In admits steam only, one way in; Water Out passes fresh water only, one way out; both with no bias.

For active, normally simulated vehicles, these formulas run once per nominal 1/60-second simulation update. Multiply per-update amounts by 60 for amounts per simulated second. families.summary: Insertion follows Insertion Target, clamped to 0 to 1, by at most 0.005 per update (a full stroke takes 3.333 s); each coupled fuel assembly scales the reaction above 0.1 × fuel by 1 − 0.01 × the summed insertion.

sections.title: Setup and interactions
sections.body: Couple it to fuel assemblies through its side couplings and drive Insertion Target, for example from an assembly's Fuel Rod Temperature.

sections.title: Insertion
sections.body: Native nuclear type 2, which the editor names control rod. While undamaged, each update I moves toward clamp(Insertion Target, 0, 1) by at most 0.005: 0.3 per simulated second, 200 updates or 3.333 s for a full stroke. The Insertion output is I. A damaged control rod skips this step, so its insertion stays where it was.

sections.title: Effect on the reaction
sections.body: Every coupled assembly adds 0.25 × I per control rod and multiplies the sum by 0.04, so each rod contributes 0.01 × I to C in b + (1 − 0.01 × C) × (B − b). Larger insertion lowers the reaction, but full insertion of one rod removes only 1% of the part above b per update. How many fuel neighbours an assembly has matters as much (see the fuel assembly page): with two, c × I above 0.0001 settles the reaction; with three, above 0.1995. In the report's 2 by 2 block with one control rod per assembly, coolant at 20: I = 0.1: r 0.2998, T 34.98; I = 0.25: r 0.1798, T 28.98; I = 1: r 0.1198, T 25.99.

findings.label: Settling and runaway layouts
findings.value: n = 2: c × I > 0.0001; n = 3: c × I > 0.1995; n = 4: no slot for a control rod
findings.detail: Inference from the assembly and rod steps for equal rods, each with n fuel neighbours and c control rods at insertion I, F held fixed: a disturbance grows by g = 0.999 × (1 − 0.01 × c × I) × (0.002 × n + 0.997002) per update. With g < 1 the reaction settles at r = b + 0.001998 × (1 − 0.01 × c × I) × b × (n − 1) ÷ (1 − g), b = 0.1 × F; otherwise it climbs to the cap of 50. A lone rod settles at 0.04999 (T 22.5 in the coolant case) and a rod with one neighbour at 0.1 (T 25), whatever the insertion. Two neighbours give g = 1.000000998 at I = 0, growing by a factor e in about 4.6 simulated hours; any c × I above 0.0001 settles them. Three neighbours need c × I above 0.1995. Four fuel neighbours fill all four couplings, so g = 1.004: ×1.27 per simulated second, from 0.1 to the cap in about 26 s. In a finite block the outer rods have fewer neighbours, so the block behaves like an n between its smallest and largest neighbour count. Report: investigation/nuclear.md. Inputs: native:stormworks64.exe:f9206d85c82f:0x14041dc40@0x14041e97f, native:stormworks64.exe:f9206d85c82f:0x14041dc40@0x14041e9e3, native:stormworks64.exe:f9206d85c82f:0x14041dc40@0x14041ea07, native:stormworks64.exe:f9206d85c82f:0x14041dc40@0x14041ea3c, native:stormworks64.exe:f9206d85c82f:0x14041dc40@0x14041ea64, native:stormworks64.exe:f9206d85c82f:0x14041dc40@0x14041ea76, native:stormworks64.exe:f9206d85c82f:0x14041dc40@0x14041dfb0, native:stormworks64.exe:f9206d85c82f:0x14041dc40@0x14041dfd3, resource:rom/data/definitions/steam_nuclear_fuel_assembly.xml:110190bc94e5:L221-L232, derived:6e6053727d4e, derived:7d3ff454a23f.

limitations: Static analysis of one build; no game process was run. Reaction, temperature, contamination and detector readings are the game's internal values: reaction is a rate, not a power in watts, and the detector reading has no stated dose unit.
Open questions about update order, contamination decay, dose units and the damage event are listed in the Nuclear fuel assemblies and control rods mechanics article.

For active, normally simulated vehicles, these formulas run once per nominal 1/60-second simulation update. Multiply per-update amounts by 60 for amounts per simulated second. A constant relaxation fraction k leaves (1-k)^60 of a gap after one simulated second. Physics solver substeps and render frames are separate; pauses, sleeping, unloaded vehicles and real-time slowdown are outside this conversion.

families.summary: Runs the reaction of the fuel rod inside it: relaxes it toward 0.1 × fuel fraction, adds the reactions of coupled fuel assemblies, scales the excess by 1 − 0.01 × the summed insertion of coupled control rods, and trades heat with the liquid in its compartment.

sections.title: Setup and interactions
sections.body: Insert a fuel rod, couple the assembly to other assemblies and control rods through its four side couplings, and read Fuel Rod Temperature to drive the control rods' Insertion Target.

sections.title: Reaction step
sections.body: Native nuclear type 0, which the editor names fuel assembly. Each update an assembly with a rod works on that rod's reaction R and fuel fraction F, with b = 0.1 × F. It computes A = b + 0.999 × (R − b), then B = S + 0.998 × (A − S), where S is the sum of R over coupled assemblies that hold a rod, and stores b + (1 − 0.01 × C) × (B − b) as the rod's working reaction, C being the summed insertion of coupled control rods (each adds 0.25 × I, scaled by 0.04). The rod then applies its own step and the 0 to 50 clamp, and after the update pass the assembly copies the result into R. Neighbours are added, not averaged, and an assembly without a rod adds nothing. Control rods scale only the part above b, so even full insertion leaves the baseline.

sections.title: Neighbours
sections.body: The assembly reads only the four couplings of type control_rod named x+, x-, z+ and z-; there is no distance search. Each coupling holds a fuel assembly or a control rod, so an assembly with four fuel neighbours has no coupling left for a control rod. The couplings sit at (0, 6, 0) on the assembly and (0, 0, 0) on the control rod, with orientations 0, 1, 4 and 5 and alignment required; none is diagonal. Two couplings link only when each sits exactly at the other's grid cell plus its outward direction, one cell apart and facing each other, with alignment vectors equal or exactly opposite. There is no distance or angle tolerance. Inference: in a normal block grid the neighbours are the four horizontal cardinal cells, and a control rod between two assemblies counts for both.

sections.title: Settling and runaway layouts
sections.body: Inference from these steps, for equal rods with n fuel neighbours and c control rods at insertion I and fuel held fixed: a disturbance grows by g = 0.999 × (1 − 0.01 × c × I) × (0.002 × n + 0.997002) per update. With g < 1 the reaction settles; otherwise it climbs to the cap of 50. A rod with no or one fuel neighbour always settles, at 0.04999 and 0.1. With two neighbours any c × I above 0.0001 settles it; with three, c × I must exceed 0.1995. Four fuel neighbours leave no coupling for a control rod and climb from 0.1 to the cap in about 26 simulated seconds. Lines and two-wide blocks therefore stay controllable; a full grid with enclosed assemblies does not. In the report's 2 by 2 block with one control rod per assembly, coolant at 20: I = 0.1: r 0.2998, T 34.98; I = 0.25: r 0.1798, T 28.98; I = 1: r 0.1198, T 25.99.

sections.title: Coolant
sections.body: With a rod inserted and the assembly's compartment holding a total amount A above 1, each update k = 0.001 × (q ÷ A) × w, where q is the compartment's liquid amount (every liquid counts alike) and w the share of the rod span, 2 to 11 blocks along the assembly axis, below the fill level y_min + (y_max − y_min) × q ÷ V. From the old temperatures the coolant moves k × (rod − coolant) and the rod moves min(q ÷ 100 × k, 0.5) × (coolant − rod). Inference: below that cap the exchange conserves q × T_coolant + 100 × T_rod, so per degree the rod holds as much heat as 100 liquid amount. Reading the fill level from the compartment bounds is also an inference. The coolant also gains 0.001 × the rod's working reaction ÷ A of radiation contamination per update, which a radiation detector in that compartment reads.

sections.title: Fuel Rod Temperature
sections.body: The output is the inserted rod's temperature after the coolant step, or 0 with no rod.

findings.label: Settling and runaway layouts
findings.value: n = 2: c × I > 0.0001; n = 3: c × I > 0.1995; n = 4: no slot for a control rod
findings.detail: Inference from the assembly and rod steps for equal rods, each with n fuel neighbours and c control rods at insertion I, F held fixed: a disturbance grows by g = 0.999 × (1 − 0.01 × c × I) × (0.002 × n + 0.997002) per update. With g < 1 the reaction settles at r = b + 0.001998 × (1 − 0.01 × c × I) × b × (n − 1) ÷ (1 − g), b = 0.1 × F; otherwise it climbs to the cap of 50. A lone rod settles at 0.04999 (T 22.5 in the coolant case) and a rod with one neighbour at 0.1 (T 25), whatever the insertion. Two neighbours give g = 1.000000998 at I = 0, growing by a factor e in about 4.6 simulated hours; any c × I above 0.0001 settles them. Three neighbours need c × I above 0.1995. Four fuel neighbours fill all four couplings, so g = 1.004: ×1.27 per simulated second, from 0.1 to the cap in about 26 s. In a finite block the outer rods have fewer neighbours, so the block behaves like an n between its smallest and largest neighbour count. Report: investigation/nuclear.md. limitations: Static analysis of one build; no game process was run. Reaction, temperature, contamination and detector readings are the game's internal values: reaction is a rate, not a power in watts, and the detector reading has no stated dose unit.
Open questions about update order, contamination decay, dose units and the damage event are listed in the Nuclear fuel assemblies and control rods mechanics article.

For active, normally simulated vehicles, these formulas run once per nominal 1/60-second simulation update. Multiply per-update amounts by 60 for amounts per simulated second. A constant relaxation fraction k leaves (1-k)^60 of a gap after one simulated second. Physics solver substeps and render frames are separate; pauses, sleeping, unloaded vehicles and real-time slowdown are outside this conversion.

families.summary: Its reaction r, 0 to 50, heats it by 0.1 × r and burns 1e-8 × r of its fuel per update: a full rod held at the cap lasts 9.259 simulated hours. Above 1500 it takes damage.

sections.title: Setup and interactions
sections.body: Insert it into a fuel assembly. Spawned with full fuel its fuel fraction F is 1: the resource initializer divides its fuel quantity by its voxel count.

sections.title: Reaction rate
sections.body: Native nuclear type 1, which the editor names fuel rod. After its assembly's step the rod sets r = clamp(b + 0.999 × (next − b), 0, 50), with b = 0.1 × F and next the working reaction. A rod outside an assembly first copies next into its reaction and multiplies next by 0.999, so its reaction decays. r is a rate in the game's own scale, not a power.

sections.title: Heat and fuel
sections.body:
Each update T rises by 0.1 × r and F falls by 1e-8 × r, then T moves 0.001 of the way toward the surrounding temperature, which the rod samples every 16 updates and ramps over 16 like the heat exchangers. Insertion acts only through r. At a constant r a full rod lasts 33333 s (9.259 simulated hours) at r = 50 and 1666667 s (463 hours) at r = 1. Inference: immersed in coolant held at Ta (liquid and total amount 100), T settles at Ta + 0.0999 × r ÷ 0.001999, about Ta + 49.975 × r; with no coolant exchange at Ta + 99.9 × r. At the cap and Ta = 20 that is 2518.7 in coolant, above the damage limit.

Above 50 °C the rod is also a local heat source of strength 0.25 × min(T − 50, 500) for the surrounding-temperature samples of parts in its own compartment. The decoded branch updates the source only above 50 and contains no reset for a rod that cools.

sections.title: Damage
sections.body: When T is strictly above 1500 after heating, the first such update raises damage by 1 and then every 300 hot updates (5 simulated seconds) add 1 more, up to 50. Cooling does not reset that counter. Damage d also removes 0.0001 × min(0.1 × d, 1) fuel per update while F is larger, up to 0.006 per simulated second, and deposits 10 times that as persistent contamination at the rod. From damage 2 a one-time event runs when the engine_overheating and vehicle_damage settings are both on; its save flag is named fire. Nothing in the rod update explodes at 1500: the threshold only drives damage.

sections.title: Radiation
sections.body: While r is above 0.001 the rod is a live source of strength s = 0.1 × r at its position; at or below it the source is removed. A detector in the same compartment at distance d reads s × (1 − d ÷ (10 × s)) out to 10 × s metres, so the reach in metres equals r: 5 at the rod and 2.5 at 25 m for r = 50. In another compartment the reach drops by 200 m, so the live source does not reach it. Sources add, with linear falloff.

limitations: Static analysis of one build; no game process was run. Reaction, temperature, contamination and detector readings are the game's internal values: reaction is a rate, not a power in watts, and the detector reading has no stated dose unit.
Open questions about update order, contamination decay, dose units and the damage event are listed in the Nuclear fuel assemblies and control rods mechanics article.

For active, normally simulated vehicles, these formulas run once per nominal 1/60-second simulation update. Multiply per-update amounts by 60 for amounts per simulated second. A constant relaxation fraction k leaves (1-k)^60 of a gap after one simulated second. Physics solver substeps and render frames are separate; pauses, sleeping, unloaded vehicles and real-time slowdown are outside this conversion.

families.summary: Adds 1000 × the steam it passes to its speed each update, keeps 0.985 of it and submits it as target RPS with weight 65 per port; steam flows only from Steam In to Steam Out.

sections.title: Flow
sections.body: Gas passes from Steam In to Steam Out one way, through the pump solver with flow factor 0.0025 and no bias. Exhaust pressure at or above inlet pressure stops it, and the turbine consumes no steam.

sections.title: Speed
sections.body: Each update the speed gains 1000 × the steam moved, 600 × at damage 1 to 19 and nothing from damage 20, is multiplied by 0.985 and is submitted as target RPS on both RPS ports with weight 65. The shaft group's speed then replaces it, so loads slow it. Unloaded, a steady steam step q settles at 0.985 ÷ 0.015 × 1000 × q (inference).

sections.title: Example
sections.body: Pure steam networks of volume 4 at pressures 2 and 1 move at most (2 - 1) ÷ 24000 per update, 0.0025 per simulated second, which settles at 2.736111 RPS. More pressure difference moves more steam, up to the solver's limits.

limitations: Open items for the whole steam cycle are listed under Steam on the parts index.
Static analysis of one build. Temperatures, pressures, amounts and speeds are the game's internal values; no figure here was measured in a running game.

For active, normally simulated vehicles, these formulas run once per nominal 1/60-second simulation update. Multiply per-update amounts by 60 for amounts per simulated second. A constant relaxation fraction k leaves (1-k)^60 of a gap after one simulated second. Physics solver substeps and render frames are separate; pauses, sleeping, unloaded vehicles and real-time slowdown are outside this conversion.

families.summary: Tail rotor on the shared force-emitter law whose Yaw input sets a signed pitch from -1 to 1; at 10 RPS and pitch 1 it gives 33.907 or 66.682 internal force per RPS by air weight branch.

sections.title: Thrust and shaft load
sections.body:
Each update the part reads its published shaft speed and computes w = RPS × 0.9999, the effective pitch p = clamp(saved pitch + input, -1, 1) and the load b = (2 × w × rotation_speed × π × blade_physics_length × p × 0.75 + p × U) × blade_efficiency × B × 0.32, where U is the relative flow along the thrust axis and B the number of intact blades. With q = clamp(b × 0.5 ÷ K, -10, 10), multiplied by 10 when the hub is below the water surface, it removes w × (1 - 1 ÷ (1 + q²)) RPS from its own speed and pushes with T = 1500 × K × removed RPS × efficiency, signed by the pitch.

force_emitter_default_pitch is 0, so the Yaw input is the effective pitch: 0 gives no thrust and no load, and the sign sets the push direction. Drive it from the main rotor's engine and feed the gyro's stabilised yaw.

sections.title: Figures
sections.body:
Rotor (Tail): K 4 or 2, 33.907 or 66.682 per RPS. Figures are raw internal force per input RPS at 10 published RPS, effective pitch 1, 4 intact blades and no inflow, before the application cap.

Air parts take one of two solver weights, K = F ÷ 1000 or F × B ÷ 8000, depending on a definition byte the decode could not tie to a resource field; each figure gives both, the first for F ÷ 1000.

sections.title: Water and altitude
sections.body: With the hub below the water surface it pushes not at all and its load ratio is multiplied by 10. Thrust is multiplied by (1 - 2.2413793e-5 × y)^5.3595023 of the vehicle's altitude y: 1 at sea level, 0 above 40000.

limitations: Internal force units before the 100 × S application cap. Open items shared by every propeller and rotor are listed under Propulsion.

For active, normally simulated vehicles, these formulas run once per nominal 1/60-second simulation update. Multiply per-update amounts by 60 for amounts per simulated second. A constant relaxation fraction k leaves (1-k)^60 of a gap after one simulated second. Physics solver substeps and render frames are separate; pauses, sleeping, unloaded vehicles and real-time slowdown are outside this conversion.

families.summary: Reads the enclosed space it sits in, or ambient air outside any enclosure, in Celsius.

sections.title: Setup and interactions
sections.body: Place it inside the compartment you want to read; outside any enclosure it reports ambient air at its location.

findings.label: Temperature Probe · tooltip
findings.value: A sensor that outputs the current temperature of an enclosed space in Celcius, if not within an enclosed volume it outputs the ambient air temperature at its location.
findings.detail: temperature_probe: developer-authored description; intended behaviour, not a measurement.

families.summary: Couples RPS A and RPS B at ratio 1 with strength e × clamp(Clutch Pressure, 0, 1)^6, set directly each update with no slew.

sections.title: Engagement
sections.body: Each update the clutch clamps Clutch Pressure to 0 to 1 as u and sets both bridge fractions to c = e × u^6, where e = min(1, a ÷ 0.01) and a = max(0, (300 - EMP count) ÷ 300) × charge fraction, or 1 with infinite electricity. Input 0.5 gives c = 1/64 and input 1 gives 1. There is no slew: a new input takes effect in the same update. It also requests 0.001 × |previous c - e × u³| electricity.

sections.title: Coupling
sections.body:
The shaft solver crosses the clutch with path weight h = 0.95 × c and ratio 1, and adds nothing while h is at or below 0.001. An isolated clutch therefore transfers nothing below input 0.3189. Above that, the two sides' speeds mix by solver weight as at a gearbox; there is no slip threshold. Example from rest at input 0.5, A with one part of weight 200 at 30 RPS and B with one part of weight 100 at 0 RPS: one pass gives A 29.63 and B 0.8565 RPS.

Any nonzero damage sets c to 0. The modular engine clutch is a different component with a cubed target and a 0.1 per update slew.

sections.title: Torque meter readings
sections.body: A torque meter's RPS output copies the group speed. Its Torque output is the group's effective solver weight I + D, not newton-metres, so meters on both sides of a gearbox or clutch do not measure the torque it transmits.

findings.label: Clutch coupling examples
findings.value: input 0.5 → c = 1/64; no coupling below input 0.3189
findings.detail: At full availability c = u⁶: input 0.5 gives 0.015625 = 1/64 and input 1 gives 1. The path weight 0.95 × c must exceed 0.001, so with an isolated clutch input below (0.001 ÷ 0.95)^(1/6) = 0.3189 transfers nothing. That threshold comes from the solver's path cutoff, not from a clamp on the input. The modular clutch instead targets u³ and moves by at most 0.1 per update. Report: investigation/transmission.md. findings.label: Two groups across one bridge
findings.value: A' = (I_A v_A + sign(q) I_B v_B h) ÷ (I_A + I_B h |q|); B' = (I_B v_B + sign(q) I_A v_A h) ÷ (I_B + I_A h ÷ |q|)

findings.label: Component updates per simulated second

families.summary: Pulses up to 6 times a second, slower as the nearest transponder gets farther: 2.4 Hz at 1000 m, 0.2927 Hz at 10000 m.

sections.title: Operating conditions
sections.body: Needs power and Active. Signal strength decreases with distance; the pulse frequency encodes distance to the nearest transponder.

sections.title: Pulse rate
sections.body:
Each update the locator takes the nearest transponder's 1 ÷ (0.002 d + 0.5) for distance d in metres, multiplies it by a noise factor 1 + n × 0.0078125 × 0.1, clamps the result to 0 to 1 and adds it to an accumulator. When the accumulator reaches 10 it drops by 10 and Transponder Pulse is on for that update.

Without noise that is 6 Hz within 250 m (a pulse every 10 updates), 2.4 Hz at 1000 m (25 updates) and 0.2927 Hz at 10000 m (205 updates). Only the nearest transponder counts; several do not add up. The part's radar_range of 20000 is not a cutoff in this loop.

sections.title: Noise
sections.body:
The noise value n comes from a smooth-noise helper with periods 128 and 128, evaluated at a clock counter, at Y = 1. It does not depend on where the transponders are or how far away they are, and one factor multiplies the nearest transponder's term after it is chosen. The scene update advances that counter by the clock multiplier, 1 at start, times the tick difference since its last step. So the pulse rate wobbles over time in a deterministic pattern rather than with a random draw per update; for small counter values it repeats every 128 counter steps (inference from the reduced model in investigation/force-cap.md). Over those 128 phases the factor stays between 0.98611 and 1.0155.

Every transponder entry in the shared list counts, whatever its channel or line of sight: the loop tests only that the entry is present. A transponder that is switched off or loses power marks its entry inactive and releases its component handle, but the locator does not read that mark.
