families.summary: A deprecated classic engine left out of the component catalog: the same update as the diesel engines with shaft weight 50, but no fuel, air, coolant or exhaust port and a starter factor of 0.

sections.title: How the update works
sections.body: turbine.xml has component type 5, so the game builds it with the same constructor and update as the diesel engines, not the jet update. engine_max_force 100000 gives shaft weight W = 50 at Max Power 100 %. Throttle is clamped to 0 to 1, although the tooltip describes -1 to 1, and the RPS Limiter, 0.99 retention, heating and overheat rules match the diesels.

sections.title: Why it does not run on its own
sections.body: The definition has four ports: RPS, Starter, Throttle and Electric. Nothing connects to the internal diesel or intake compartments: the constructor clears them and the current serializer does not save them, so the supply gate holds the effective throttle at 0. Only the coolant compartment starts filled, with 100 L of fresh water. electric_magnitude 0 makes the starter request 0, even with infinite electricity. Derived from the traced paths, not tested in game: a new turbine at rest does not start itself. With infinite_fuel on and its shaft spun above 2 RPS by another component, it gains speed like a diesel with W = 50.

sections.title: Shaft and load
sections.body: It still exchanges speed with its shaft group at weight 50, so on a shared shaft it adds 0.99 retention like any classic engine and heats at 0.0075 × |r| °C per update.

sections.title: Availability
sections.body: turbine.xml carries definition flags 537133056, which include the Deprecated bit. The game appends " (Deprecated)" to the name of every part with that bit, and leaves such parts out of the component catalog rebuild, the research and catalog state and the component list for existing vehicles. None of these tests checks career or creative mode, so the Turbine Engine cannot be picked from the normal component catalog in any mode.

limitations: Static analysis of one build; the game was not run. How old saves migrate a legacy turbine, whether loading an older vehicle or a special spawning path can still place one, and whether an indirect world, editor or script writer fills its private compartments, was not traced.

For active, normally simulated vehicles, these formulas run once per nominal 1/60-second simulation update. Multiply per-update amounts by 60 for amounts per simulated second. A constant relaxation fraction k leaves (1-k)^60 of a gap after one simulated second. Physics solver substeps and render frames are separate; pauses, sleeping, unloaded vehicles and real-time slowdown are outside this conversion.

families.summary: Reels 0.24 m/s at Speed 1 and full electricity (0.024 to 1.2 m/s over the editor range 0.1 to 5), between 0.25 m and its 16 m cable_length.

sections.title: Reel speed
sections.body: Each update a held Hose Up shortens the hose by 0.004 × Speed × p metres and Hose Down lengthens it by the same, p being the fraction of a 0.01 charge request the electric network supplies. At the default Speed 1 and full supply that is 0.24 m/s, the same for every legacy winch and the Hose whatever its length. The Speed property runs from 0.1 to 5 in the editor, 0.024 to 1.2 m/s. A charge shortage or EMP lowers p and slows the reel in proportion. These rates change the hose's rest length; a loaded end piece can lag behind it (inference).

sections.title: Length limits
sections.body: After each update the rest length is clamped to between 0.25 m and its cable_length, 16 m, both inclusive. A geometric guard can raise the lower bound: the distance between the two attachment points divided by cable_length, capped at 1, minus 0.1 (0.01 in component states above 1), used directly as metres. The reel reads no other end, so its own cable_length is the whole limit. Hose Length outputs the clamped rest length.

sections.title: Both controls and electricity
sections.body: Each held control makes its own 0.01 charge request every update, Hose Up first, also while the hose sits at a limit. One control at full supply asks for 0.6 charge units per simulated second and both for 1.2. With full supply both steps cancel. Under shortage Hose Up is served first: with 0.015 units in the pool Hose Up gets the whole step and Hose Down half of it, so the hose shortens by 0.002 m at Speed 1. Speed changes the distance per request, not the request.

sections.title: Fluid through the hose
sections.body: The Hose links the fluid network at its base (Fluid) to the one at its end piece through the two-port solver: bias 0, both directions, factor 1, all species. It adds no compartment of its own, and the exchange does not read the current length, so a longer hose neither stores more fluid nor restricts flow more.

limitations: The decoded reel and rope code has no maximum tension or snapping threshold. Rope stiffness and any cap or severing path elsewhere in the solver are listed as open items in the Winch controls, length and hose connections mechanics article.
Static analysis of one build. Reel rates are changes of the rope's rest length; no loaded hook travel was measured in a running game.

For active, normally simulated vehicles, these formulas run once per nominal 1/60-second simulation update. Multiply per-update amounts by 60 for amounts per simulated second. A constant relaxation fraction k leaves (1-k)^60 of a gap after one simulated second. Physics solver substeps and render frames are separate; pauses, sleeping, unloaded vehicles and real-time slowdown are outside this conversion.

families.summary: End piece of the legacy Hose Winch: the rope's far attachment and fluid end, with no reel of its own.

sections.title: Role
sections.body: Hose (water_hose, 16 m) names this definition as child_name. The winch builds a Bullet soft-body rope from the winch's attachment point to this piece's, and links its Fluid port to this piece's Fluid port with factor 1. The winch owns Up, Down, Speed, the length limits and the charge requests, so this piece moves at its winch's rate, 0.24 m/s at Speed 1 and full supply. Its own cable_length 0 does not limit the winch's rope, and it has no reel or controls.

families.summary: Hold either interact action to pump: bias 3, one-way, with a handle factor that eases over 60 controller updates; at most 60 L/s at equal pressure.

sections.title: Operating conditions
sections.body: Holding an interact action sets the handle target to 1, and the handle factor h eases toward it over 60 controller updates. While h is above 0.01 the pump calls the two-port solver with bias pump_pressure = 3 and factor h, one-way, all species. Released, h eases back, and at or below 0.01 nothing moves. The pump holds no fluid; its ports connect straight to the pipe networks.

sections.title: Handle easing
sections.body: When the target changes, the controller keeps the current factor as a, takes the new target b and restarts its count t at 0. Then h = a + (b − a) × E(t ÷ 60), with E(u) = 2u² for u < 0.5 and E(u) = 1 − 2(1 − u)² from 0.5 to 1: slow at both ends and fastest halfway. On the update with t = 0 it keeps h. At t = 60, or once the remaining difference is 0.001 or less, h snaps to the target. Letting go before the handle is fully up restarts the curve from the current factor. From rest h is 0.0139 at t = 5, the first count above the 0.01 pumping threshold, and 0.5 at t = 30.

sections.title: Flow
sections.body: At equal pressure between two pipe networks the bound is min(3, 20) ÷ 30 = 0.1 amount per update, 60 L/s at h = 1, against 200 L/s for the small electric pump. Backpressure, fill and other ports lower it, and backpressure cannot reverse it.

families.summary: Fills its enclosing custom compartment with up to 0.99 × fill × volume of the selected fluid, limited by free room: most fluids at the first build, diesel and jet fuel through a vehicle spawn's fuel fill.

sections.title: Operating conditions
sections.body: On the first build the spawner adds min(free room, 0.99 × fill × V) of the selected fluid to the compartment it sits in, where V is that compartment's volume. Air is split into nitrogen, oxygen and CO2. Diesel and jet fuel are skipped by this branch. Its tooltip says gases are spawned compressed at 60 atm; under the pressure law a compartment whose gas reaches A = V reads 60 atm.

sections.title: Diesel and jet fuel
sections.body: Diesel and jet fuel are added by the request-gated fuel fill of a vehicle spawn, the same operation that fills diesel and jet-fuel tanks (see Fluid Tank). For a spawner with an enclosing compartment C it adds q = min(C.V − C.A, 0.99 × fill × C.V) of the selected fuel to C. On the inventory branch q is first capped to that fuel in stock, which then loses q. The fuel is added to what C already holds, so q depends on earlier fills, other spawners and restored contents. Unlike a fuel tank, the spawner gets no air with it.

findings.label: Compartment pressure law
findings.detail: All 13 fluid indices (0 to 12) enter only as liquid sum L or gas sum G, with A = L + G. Pure gas reduces to P = 60 × A ÷ V at any volume. Pure liquid in a volume up to 8 (80 L), such as a pipe network of 4, also gives 60 × A ÷ V. Pure liquid above volume 8 gives max(0.5 × A ÷ V, 7.5 × (A − V + 8)): under 0.5 atm until less than 8 (80 L) of room is left, then 7.5 atm per amount (per 75 L) up to 60 at full. Temperature does not enter. Inference from the instruction sequence; degenerate states follow the original SSE arithmetic. Report: investigation/fluids-network.md. families.summary: Reels 0.24 m/s at Speed 1 and full electricity (0.024 to 1.2 m/s over the editor range 0.1 to 5), between 0.25 m and its 20 m cable_length.

sections.title: Reel speed
sections.body: Each update a held Up shortens the rope by 0.004 × Speed × p metres and Down lengthens it by the same, p being the fraction of a 0.01 charge request the electric network supplies. At the default Speed 1 and full supply that is 0.24 m/s, the same for every legacy winch and the Hose whatever its length. The Speed property runs from 0.1 to 5 in the editor, 0.024 to 1.2 m/s. A charge shortage or EMP lowers p and slows the reel in proportion. These rates change the rope's rest length; a loaded end piece can lag behind it (inference).

sections.title: Length limits
sections.body: After each update the rest length is clamped to between 0.25 m and its cable_length, 20 m, both inclusive. A geometric guard can raise the lower bound: the distance between the two attachment points divided by cable_length, capped at 1, minus 0.1 (0.01 in component states above 1), used directly as metres. The reel reads no other end, so its own cable_length is the whole limit. Length outputs the clamped rest length.

sections.title: Both controls and electricity
sections.body: Each held control makes its own 0.01 charge request every update, Up first, also while the rope sits at a limit. One control at full supply asks for 0.6 charge units per simulated second and both for 1.2. With full supply both steps cancel. Under shortage Up is served first: with 0.015 units in the pool Up gets the whole step and Down half of it, so the rope shortens by 0.002 m at Speed 1. Speed changes the distance per request, not the request.

sections.title: Fluid through the cable
sections.body: This winch is type 20, like the Hose, and runs the same update: the Fluid port on the winch and the one on its end piece are linked through the two-port solver with bias 0, both directions and factor 1. The exchange does not read cable length and adds no hose volume.

families.summary: End piece of the legacy Medium, Large and Huge Winches: the rope's far attachment and fluid end, with no reel of its own.

sections.title: Role
sections.body: Medium Winch (winch_a, 20 m), Large Winch (winch_large_a, 100 m) and Huge Winch (winch_huge_a, 500 m) name this definition as child_name. The winch builds a Bullet soft-body rope from the winch's attachment point to this piece's, and links its Fluid port to this piece's Fluid port with factor 1. The winch owns Up, Down, Speed, the length limits and the charge requests, so this piece moves at its winch's rate, 0.24 m/s at Speed 1 and full supply. Its own cable_length 0 does not limit the winch's rope, and it has no reel or controls.

families.summary: Reels 0.24 m/s at Speed 1 and full electricity (0.024 to 1.2 m/s over the editor range 0.1 to 5), between 0.25 m and its 10 m cable_length.

sections.title: Reel speed
sections.body: Each update a held Up shortens the rope by 0.004 × Speed × p metres and Down lengthens it by the same, p being the fraction of a 0.01 charge request the electric network supplies. At the default Speed 1 and full supply that is 0.24 m/s, the same for every legacy winch and the Hose whatever its length. The Speed property runs from 0.1 to 5 in the editor, 0.024 to 1.2 m/s. A charge shortage or EMP lowers p and slows the reel in proportion. These rates change the rope's rest length; a loaded end piece can lag behind it (inference).

sections.title: Length limits
sections.body: After each update the rest length is clamped to between 0.25 m and its cable_length, 10 m, both inclusive. A geometric guard can raise the lower bound: the distance between the two attachment points divided by cable_length, capped at 1, minus 0.1 (0.01 in component states above 1), used directly as metres. The reel reads no other end, so its own cable_length is the whole limit.

sections.title: Both controls and electricity
sections.body: Each held control makes its own 0.01 charge request every update, Up first, also while the rope sits at a limit. One control at full supply asks for 0.6 charge units per simulated second and both for 1.2. With full supply both steps cancel. Under shortage Up is served first: with 0.015 units in the pool Up gets the whole step and Down half of it, so the rope shortens by 0.002 m at Speed 1. Speed changes the distance per request, not the request.

sections.title: Fluid through the cable
sections.body: This winch is type 20, like the Hose, and runs the same update: the Fluid port on the winch and the one on its end piece are linked through the two-port solver with bias 0, both directions and factor 1. The exchange does not read cable length and adds no hose volume.

sections.title: Role
sections.body: Small Winch (winch_electric, 10 m) names this definition as child_name. The winch builds a Bullet soft-body rope from the winch's attachment point to this piece's, and links its Fluid port to this piece's Fluid port with factor 1. The winch owns Up, Down, Speed, the length limits and the charge requests, so this piece moves at its winch's rate, 0.24 m/s at Speed 1 and full supply. Its own cable_length 0 does not limit the winch's rope, and it has no reel or controls.

families.summary: Reels 0.24 m/s at Speed 1 and full electricity (0.024 to 1.2 m/s over the editor range 0.1 to 5), between 0.25 m and its 500 m cable_length.

sections.title: Reel speed
sections.body: Each update a held Up shortens the rope by 0.004 × Speed × p metres and Down lengthens it by the same, p being the fraction of a 0.01 charge request the electric network supplies. At the default Speed 1 and full supply that is 0.24 m/s, the same for every legacy winch and the Hose whatever its length. The Speed property runs from 0.1 to 5 in the editor, 0.024 to 1.2 m/s. A charge shortage or EMP lowers p and slows the reel in proportion. These rates change the rope's rest length; a loaded end piece can lag behind it (inference).

sections.title: Length limits
sections.body: After each update the rest length is clamped to between 0.25 m and its cable_length, 500 m, both inclusive. A geometric guard can raise the lower bound: the distance between the two attachment points divided by cable_length, capped at 1, minus 0.1 (0.01 in component states above 1), used directly as metres. The reel reads no other end, so its own cable_length is the whole limit. Length outputs the clamped rest length.

sections.title: Both controls and electricity
sections.body: Each held control makes its own 0.01 charge request every update, Up first, also while the rope sits at a limit. One control at full supply asks for 0.6 charge units per simulated second and both for 1.2. With full supply both steps cancel. Under shortage Up is served first: with 0.015 units in the pool Up gets the whole step and Down half of it, so the rope shortens by 0.002 m at Speed 1. Speed changes the distance per request, not the request.

sections.title: Fluid through the cable
sections.body: This winch is type 20, like the Hose, and runs the same update: the Fluid port on the winch and the one on its end piece are linked through the two-port solver with bias 0, both directions and factor 1. The exchange does not read cable length and adds no hose volume.

limitations: The decoded reel and rope code has no maximum tension or snapping threshold. Rope stiffness and any cap or severing path elsewhere in the solver are listed as open items in the Winch controls, length and hose connections mechanics article.
Static analysis of one build. Reel rates are changes of the rope's rest length; no loaded hook travel was measured in a running game.

For active, normally simulated vehicles, these formulas run once per nominal 1/60-second simulation update. Multiply per-update amounts by 60 for amounts per simulated second. A constant relaxation fraction k leaves (1-k)^60 of a gap after one simulated second. Physics solver substeps and render frames are separate; pauses, sleeping, unloaded vehicles and real-time slowdown are outside this conversion.

families.summary: A winch end piece identical to winch_b; no shipped winch places it, and the Huge Winch uses winch_b.

sections.title: Role
sections.body: No shipped definition names this one as child_name: the legacy Huge Winch (winch_huge_a) names winch_b, and this file is byte-identical to winch_b. The role below is winch_b's: the winch builds a Bullet soft-body rope from the winch's attachment point to this piece's, and links its Fluid port to this piece's Fluid port with factor 1. The winch owns Up, Down, Speed, the length limits and the charge requests, so this piece moves at its winch's rate, 0.24 m/s at Speed 1 and full supply. Its own cable_length 0 does not limit the winch's rope, and it has no reel or controls.

limitations: The decoded reel and rope code has no maximum tension or snapping threshold. Rope stiffness and any cap or severing path elsewhere in the solver are listed as open items in the Winch controls, length and hose connections mechanics article.
Static analysis of one build. Reel rates are changes of the rope's rest length; no loaded hook travel was measured in a running game.

families.summary: Reels 0.24 m/s at Speed 1 and full electricity (0.024 to 1.2 m/s over the editor range 0.1 to 5), between 0.25 m and its 100 m cable_length.

sections.title: Reel speed
sections.body: Each update a held Up shortens the rope by 0.004 × Speed × p metres and Down lengthens it by the same, p being the fraction of a 0.01 charge request the electric network supplies. At the default Speed 1 and full supply that is 0.24 m/s, the same for every legacy winch and the Hose whatever its length. The Speed property runs from 0.1 to 5 in the editor, 0.024 to 1.2 m/s. A charge shortage or EMP lowers p and slows the reel in proportion. These rates change the rope's rest length; a loaded end piece can lag behind it (inference).

sections.title: Length limits
sections.body: After each update the rest length is clamped to between 0.25 m and its cable_length, 100 m, both inclusive. A geometric guard can raise the lower bound: the distance between the two attachment points divided by cable_length, capped at 1, minus 0.1 (0.01 in component states above 1), used directly as metres. The reel reads no other end, so its own cable_length is the whole limit. Length outputs the clamped rest length.

sections.title: Both controls and electricity
sections.body: Each held control makes its own 0.01 charge request every update, Up first, also while the rope sits at a limit. One control at full supply asks for 0.6 charge units per simulated second and both for 1.2. With full supply both steps cancel. Under shortage Up is served first: with 0.015 units in the pool Up gets the whole step and Down half of it, so the rope shortens by 0.002 m at Speed 1. Speed changes the distance per request, not the request.

sections.title: Fluid through the cable
sections.body: This winch is type 20, like the Hose, and runs the same update: the Fluid port on the winch and the one on its end piece are linked through the two-port solver with bias 0, both directions and factor 1. The exchange does not read cable length and adds no hose volume.

families.summary: A winch end piece identical to winch_b; no shipped winch places it, and the Large Winch uses winch_b.

sections.title: Role
sections.body: No shipped definition names this one as child_name: the legacy Large Winch (winch_large_a) names winch_b, and this file is byte-identical to winch_b. The role below is winch_b's: the winch builds a Bullet soft-body rope from the winch's attachment point to this piece's, and links its Fluid port to this piece's Fluid port with factor 1. The winch owns Up, Down, Speed, the length limits and the charge requests, so this piece moves at its winch's rate, 0.24 m/s at Speed 1 and full supply. Its own cable_length 0 does not limit the winch's rope, and it has no reel or controls.

families.summary: Shares one 40 L fluid network between Fluid Node 1 and Fluid Node 2 and exchanges with linked hoses at factor 1.

sections.title: Operating conditions
sections.body: The extra network builder gives a subtype 8 pulley one network of volume 4, 40 L, and registers both fluid ports in it, so fluid passes through the pulley freely. Exchanges started from the pulley use factor 1 instead of the hose links' 0.5. The network's volume does not change with deployed hose length.

sections.title: Linked side
sections.body: A hook linked to the pulley picks the pulley's port by the reciprocal attachment pointer: when the pulley's back pointer leads to that hook it uses the pulley's second fluid port, otherwise its first. As for every hose link, only the end holding the exchange flag runs the exchange.

families.summary: Shares one 40 L fluid network between Fluid Node 1 and Fluid Node 2 and exchanges with linked hoses at factor 1.

sections.title: Operating conditions
sections.body: The extra network builder gives a subtype 8 pulley one network of volume 4, 40 L, and registers both fluid ports in it, so fluid passes through the pulley freely. Exchanges started from the pulley use factor 1 instead of the hose links' 0.5. The network's volume does not change with deployed hose length.

sections.title: Linked side
sections.body: A hook linked to the pulley picks the pulley's port by the reciprocal attachment pointer: when the pulley's back pointer leads to that hook it uses the pulley's second fluid port, otherwise its first. As for every hose link, only the end holding the exchange flag runs the exchange.

families.summary: Cools its fluid toward the surrounding temperature at 0.003 per update, more when exposed to airflow.

sections.title: Operating conditions
sections.body: The passive radiator shares case 9 with the electric radiators and the fluid heat sink. Without a fan, its only boost is airflow: outside an enclosed compartment the multiplier becomes 1 + min(2, air speed ÷ 40), with air speed in m/s relative to the wind, so it reaches 3 at 80 m/s.

sections.title: Setup and interactions
sections.body: Connect both fluid ports; with either port unconnected the cooling step is skipped. Place it on the exterior of a moving vehicle to use the airflow term.

sections.title: Per-second rate
sections.body: At 60 updates per simulated second the passive term leaves 0.835 of the gap to ambient after one second (time constant 5.55 s). At the airflow cap the multiplier is 3, which leaves 0.581 (1.84 s).

sections.title: Volume
sections.body: The compartment volume equals the listed voxels, 9 units of 10 L.

sections.title: Flow through the radiator
sections.body:
Each update the radiator exchanges with its Fluid A network, then its Fluid B network, then cools. Arriving water is mixed by the radiator's amount after the move, and below 0.01 amount per update a direct exchange also moves temperature through the ports. Its volume is capacity: in a pumped loop it need not stay full, and its water settles cooler than the coolant manifold.

For one radiator fed at a fixed inlet temperature with flow q and stored water A, the outlet sits q ÷ (k × A + (1 + k) × q) of the way from ambient to the inlet, with k = 0.003 × (1 + fan). With 9 units of water, 200 L/s and a full fan that is 83.90 °C out for 100 °C in at 20 °C ambient, a 16.10 °C drop. The cooling capacity calculator's finite-flow mode steps whole loops.

sections.title: Surrounding temperature
sections.body: The radiator cools toward the same surrounding temperature the heat exchangers use. It samples it at its own position every 16 updates and ramps to each new sample over 16 updates. Outside a compartment the sample blends the air and water weather temperatures by depth; inside an enclosed compartment it is the compartment's temperature. Nearby heat sources raise it. The weather temperature follows the region, season, time of day, rain and height; the Heat exchange category summarizes it and the Weather temperature, lighting and hazards mechanics article gives the equations.

findings.value: T_out - T_amb = q ÷ (k × A + (1 + k) × q) × (T_in - T_amb)

For active, normally simulated vehicles, these formulas run once per nominal 1/60-second simulation update. Multiply per-update amounts by 60 for amounts per simulated second. families.summary: Underwater propellers whose Pitch input sets a normalized pitch from -1 to 1; solver weight K = F × B ÷ 8000 (10, 40 and 80 with 4 intact blades); 4073.904, 20411.306 and 35002.234 per RPS at 10 RPS and pitch 1.

sections.title: How pitch works
sections.body:
The definitions carry no force_emitter_default_pitch, so the saved pitch starts at 0 and the Pitch input is the effective pitch p, clamped to -1 to 1. It is a normalized number, not a blade angle in degrees or turns. p = 0 gives no load and no thrust, the sign of p sets the direction, and |p| scales both the speed taken from the shaft and the push.

Each update the part reads its published shaft speed and computes w = RPS × 0.9999, the effective pitch p = clamp(saved pitch + input, -1, 1) and the load b = (2 × w × rotation_speed × π × blade_physics_length × p × 0.75 + p × U) × blade_efficiency × B × 0.32, where U is the relative flow along the thrust axis and B the number of intact blades. With q = clamp(b × 0.5 ÷ K, -10, 10), multiplied by 10 when the hub is below the water surface, it removes w × (1 - 1 ÷ (1 + q²)) RPS from its own speed and pushes with T = 1500 × K × removed RPS × efficiency, signed by the pitch.

sections.title: Sizes
sections.body:
Small Pitchable Propeller: K 10, 4073.904 per RPS, 2.7159 RPS removed; Pitchable Propeller: K 40, 20411.306 per RPS, 3.4019 RPS removed; Large Pitchable Propeller: K 80, 35002.234 per RPS, 2.9169 RPS removed. Figures are raw internal force per input RPS at 10 published RPS, effective pitch 1, 4 intact blades and no inflow, before the application cap.

Their weight counts intact blades: each lost blade lowers K and the load by one quarter of the 4-blade value.

sections.title: Water and flow
sections.body: The hub must be at or below the sampled water surface for thrust; under water q is multiplied by 10. U comes from the propeller's own velocity through still water, signed by the pitch.

For active, normally simulated vehicles, these formulas run once per nominal 1/60-second simulation update. Multiply per-update amounts by 60 for amounts per simulated second. families.summary: Plain type-9 part: the shared basic component class, ordinary collision voxels and buoyancy surfaces, no window-specific update.

sections.title: Component class
sections.body: Every variant has type 9. The component factory gives type 9 the basic component class, which has no per-update callback, so the window runs no code of its own each update.

families.summary: Burns trunc(400 × w² × burn rate) + 1 fuel units per update and pushes with 60 times that; at burn rate 1 a full nozzle plus one matching fuel section burns 300 updates (5 s), the small size 100 updates.

sections.title: Fuel use and thrust
sections.body: Each burning update uses q = min(D, fuel left) units with D = trunc(400 × w² × burn rate) + 1, w the nozzle width in voxels, and pushes along its axis with raw thrust 60 × q. At burn rate 1: Small: D 401, raw thrust 24060, 50 updates with no section and 100 with one; Medium: D 3601, raw thrust 216060, 150 updates with no section and 300 with one; Large: D 10001, raw thrust 600060, 150 updates with no section and 300 with one; Huge: D 19601, raw thrust 1176060, 150 updates with no section and 300 with one. The last update can push less.

sections.title: Fuel and burn time
sections.body: The nozzle and every connected fuel section of rocket_type 1 add w² × h to the fuel volume, and a full load is 20000 units per volume unit. Fuel sections extend the burn without raising thrust: at burn rate 1 each matching section adds about 150 updates (2.5 s) to the medium, large and huge sizes and 50 updates to the small. Halving the burn rate roughly halves thrust and doubles the burn time.

sections.title: Burn Rate, altitude and force cap
sections.body: The Burn Rate slider runs from 1% to 100%, stored as 0.01 to 1. Thrust is multiplied by (1 - 2.2413793e-5 × y)^5.3595023 of the altitude y and is 0 above 40000. The applied force is capped at 1000 × S; control surfaces are capped at 5 × S and jet exhausts at 100 × S by the same mechanism. S is the summed adjusted mass of every body joined to this one by joints, free or locked, so all of them share one S; the Control surfaces category gives the rule and examples.

findings.label: Cap-scale group flood
findings.detail: Builds one integer label per vehicle body (assembly +0x18). For each component link it calls vtable slot +0x60, follows the counterpart at +0x150 or +0x148 to its body through component +0x28 and gives that body the same label. The flood does not test joint limits, the lock input, relative motion or motor power. Multibody joints (vtable 0x140b02a08) return themselves from slot +0x60 (0x1400cb6a0, mov rax,rcx; ret), so a pivot, hinge, piston or other multibody joint puts its two bodies in one label group, free or locked. Winches (vtable 0x140b958e8) also return themselves. The extractor re-reads these slot pointers. Report: investigation/force-cap.md. findings.value: 1000; 1001 for 1000 + 1 on one joint; 992.727273 with an auxiliary mass of 1; 1000 and 1 when not joined
findings.detail: One body of mass 1000: S = 1000, so the caps are 5 × S = 5000, 100 × S = 100000 and 1000 × S = 1000000. Bodies of 1000 and 1 joined by a joint, free or locked: T = 1001, H = 1000, D = 1000 + 1000 ÷ 40 = 1025, r = 1001 ÷ 1025, adjusted masses 976.585366 and 24.414634, S = 1001 for both bodies and an air cap of 5 × S = 5005. One body of 1000 with one auxiliary mass of 1: D = 1000 + 1000 ÷ 120, S = 992.727273 and the adjusted auxiliary mass 8.272727, together 1001. Bodies of 1000 and 1 with no joint between them: S = 1000 and S = 1. The cap applies to each force separately, so it is not a budget for the whole vehicle. Calculations from the decoded arithmetic; no game measurement. Report: investigation/force-cap.md. limitations: Forces are internal units before the 1000 × S cap. One burning nozzle per fuel group is assumed; several nozzles on one group share its fuel.

For active, normally simulated vehicles, these formulas run once per nominal 1/60-second simulation update. Multiply per-update amounts by 60 for amounts per simulated second. A constant relaxation fraction k leaves (1-k)^60 of a gap after one simulated second. Physics solver substeps and render frames are separate; pauses, sleeping, unloaded vehicles and real-time slowdown are outside this conversion.

families.summary: Each section adds 20000 × w² × h fuel units (small 20000, medium 540000, large 1500000, huge 2940000) to the nozzle it connects to, lengthening the burn without changing thrust.

sections.title: Fuel and burn time
sections.body: The nozzle and every connected fuel section of rocket_type 1 add w² × h to the fuel volume, and a full load is 20000 units per volume unit. Fuel sections extend the burn without raising thrust: at burn rate 1 each matching section adds about 150 updates (2.5 s) to the medium, large and huge sizes and 50 updates to the small. Halving the burn rate roughly halves thrust and doubles the burn time.

sections.title: Sizes
sections.body: Widths 1, 3, 5 and 7 voxels match the small, medium, large and huge nozzles. At burn rate 1 a matching section adds about 150 updates, 2.5 s, of burn to the larger sizes and 50 updates to the small one.

findings.detail: The substep is 1 ÷ the worker's solver rate (worker+0xb8), or binary32 1/60 from 0x140baf98c in the fallback branch at 0x1405e3af4. limitations: Burn time assumes one burning nozzle and full fuel.

For active, normally simulated vehicles, these formulas run once per nominal 1/60-second simulation update. Multiply per-update amounts by 60 for amounts per simulated second. A constant relaxation fraction k leaves (1-k)^60 of a gap after one simulated second. Physics solver substeps and render frames are separate; pauses, sleeping, unloaded vehicles and real-time slowdown are outside this conversion.

families.summary: Each section adds 20000 × w² × h fuel units (small 20000, medium 540000, large 1500000, huge 2940000) to the nozzle it connects to, lengthening the burn without changing thrust.

sections.title: Fuel and burn time
sections.body: The nozzle and every connected fuel section of rocket_type 1 add w² × h to the fuel volume, and a full load is 20000 units per volume unit. Fuel sections extend the burn without raising thrust: at burn rate 1 each matching section adds about 150 updates (2.5 s) to the medium, large and huge sizes and 50 updates to the small. Halving the burn rate roughly halves thrust and doubles the burn time.

sections.title: Sizes
sections.body: Widths 1, 3, 5 and 7 voxels match the small, medium, large and huge nozzles. At burn rate 1 a matching section adds about 150 updates, 2.5 s, of burn to the larger sizes and 50 updates to the small one. Finned sections hold the same fuel as plain ones.

limitations: Burn time assumes one burning nozzle and full fuel.

For active, normally simulated vehicles, these formulas run once per nominal 1/60-second simulation update. Multiply per-update amounts by 60 for amounts per simulated second. A constant relaxation fraction k leaves (1-k)^60 of a gap after one simulated second. Physics solver substeps and render frames are separate; pauses, sleeping, unloaded vehicles and real-time slowdown are outside this conversion.

families.summary: Burns at most 0.00002 × voxels coal per update, 0.054 or 0.21 per simulated second, adding 200 to the fire temperature per unit of coal burned and heating its coolant at k = 0.0008 × voxels.

sections.title: Ignition and coal
sections.body: Ignition takes one coal and sets the ignition state to 3600. The combustion code only tests whether that state is nonzero and never counts it down, so 3600 is not a burn time there. The fire also keeps burning while it is hotter than 150. Burning draws on a fractional reserve, refilled one coal at a time from the shared inventory, to which a firebox adds 10 slots.

sections.title: Burn rate
sections.body: Each update it requests 0.00002 × voxels × clamp((600 - T) ÷ 400, 0, 1) coal: 0.0009 per update for the small firebox and 0.0035 for the large while far below 600. The request falls to 0 as the fire approaches 600. Air pressure must be more than 1 above Exhaust pressure and the air must carry oxygen near the 0.21 reference; otherwise the burn is cut. Each unit of coal actually burned adds 200 to the fire temperature, and burnt oxygen leaves as carbon dioxide.

sections.title: Heat and coolant
sections.body: The fire then loses 0.001 of its gap to the surrounding temperature per update, rising toward 0.01 with damage, and exchanges heat with its coolant chamber at k = 0.0008 × voxels: 0.036 small and 0.14 large. The fire counts with weight 400 and the coolant with its stored amount, and there is no exchange below 0.1 coolant. While burning, Air pulls air in with a bias of -10 and Exhaust pushes out with +10. With both coolant ports connected, Coolant In draws fluid with a bias of -clamp(T - 50, 0, 10), so a fire hotter than 50 drives its own coolant loop (inference from the port solver's sign).

sections.title: Outputs
sections.body: Temperature reads the fire temperature, not the coolant temperature its description names, sampled before the update's burn. Coal Level is the inventory's whole item count.

sections.title: Damage
sections.body: Damage raises the ambient loss toward 0.01. A hot damaged firebox sets a pending flag, and after the update a shared helper queues a component damage event when the vehicle_damage setting is on. What that event does downstream is listed under Steam on the parts index.

limitations: Open items for the whole steam cycle are listed under Steam on the parts index.
Static analysis of one build. Temperatures, pressures, amounts and speeds are the game's internal values; no figure here was measured in a running game.

For active, normally simulated vehicles, these formulas run once per nominal 1/60-second simulation update. Multiply per-update amounts by 60 for amounts per simulated second. A constant relaxation fraction k leaves (1-k)^60 of a gap after one simulated second. Physics solver substeps and render frames are separate; pauses, sleeping, unloaded vehicles and real-time slowdown are outside this conversion.

families.summary: Switches its ports by half turn of the crank and adds 0.002 × (p_B - p_A) × sin(2πz) to its crank group each update; shaft weight 20 × voxels per port.

sections.title: Valves
sections.body: The crank phase z, wrapped to 0 to 1, opens one port per chamber: from z = 0.5 the first Steam In and the second Steam Out, below 0.5 the first Steam Out and the second Steam In. The closed ports move nothing. The port order is taken from the definition (inference). Supply steam to both Steam In ports and vent both Steam Out ports; no external valve timing is needed.

sections.title: Drive
sections.body: Each update a = 0.002 × (p_B - p_A) × sin(2πz) is added to the crank group, p being each chamber's pressure times its steam fraction. The factor is 0.0012 at damage 1 to 9. The open chamber matches the sign of the sine on each half turn, so the drive keeps one direction (inference). At damage 10 or more the update joins the two Steam In ports to each other and the two Steam Out ports to each other, bypassing the chambers, and the piston adds nothing.

sections.title: Sizes
sections.body: Chambers hold 0.0015 × voxels, 0.009, 0.1215 and 0.4275, and both RPS ports submit the group speed with weight 120, 1620 and 5700. Crank radii 0.075, 0.146 and 0.216 give geometric strokes of 0.15, 0.292 and 0.432 world units, about metres (inference from the render code).

sections.title: Crank
sections.body: At the end of each update every crank group adds the summed drive a to its speed, multiplies by 0.99, clamps the result to −10 … 10 and clears a. Its phase then advances by speed ÷ 60 turns and wraps with floor, so a crank turning backward wraps too, and the speed is in RPS, capped at 10. There is no division by an inertia sum: shaft load acts only through the port exchange, which replaces the group speed with the shaft group's published speed before this step. Unloaded, a constant drive a settles at 99 × a and reaches the cap from a = 0.10101.

sections.title: Outputs
sections.body: Piston Position is z in turns, 0 to 1, not rod extension. RPS is the crank group's speed.

Static analysis of one build. Temperatures, pressures, amounts and speeds are the game's internal values; no figure here was measured in a running game.

For active, normally simulated vehicles, these formulas run once per nominal 1/60-second simulation update. Multiply per-update amounts by 60 for amounts per simulated second. A constant relaxation fraction k leaves (1-k)^60 of a gap after one simulated second. Physics solver substeps and render frames are separate; pauses, sleeping, unloaded vehicles and real-time slowdown are outside this conversion.

families.summary: Tread speed per RPS: Tank Drive Wheel (Small) 2.513 m/s (9.048 km/h); Tank Drive Wheel (Small/Wide) 2.513 m/s (9.048 km/h); Tank Drive Wheel (Medium) 3.927 m/s (14.14 km/h); Tank Drive Wheel (Large) 3.927 m/s (14.14 km/h); Tank Drive Wheel (Huge) 6.283 m/s (22.62 km/h). Wheels in one track share one mean RPS.

sections.title: Speed per RPS
sections.body: Tank wheels use the road wheel's radius law at wheel_size 1: Tank Drive Wheel (Small) 2.513 m/s (9.048 km/h); Tank Drive Wheel (Small/Wide) 2.513 m/s (9.048 km/h); Tank Drive Wheel (Medium) 3.927 m/s (14.14 km/h); Tank Drive Wheel (Large) 3.927 m/s (14.14 km/h); Tank Drive Wheel (Huge) 6.283 m/s (22.62 km/h). Medium and Large share radius 0.625 m, Small and Small/Wide 0.4 m.

sections.title: Tracks
sections.body: Tank wheels in one track share speed by a plain mean: the track pass adds each member's signed RPS, divides by the count and writes the mean back to every member. Two members at 10 and 0 RPS both leave at 5, whatever their radii, so tank wheels of different sizes in one track turn at one RPS but their treads move at different speeds. A tank wheel keeps its tyre factor 1 inside a track and halves it outside one, and keeps 0.975 of its RPS per update in a track and 0.7 outside one; the tyre type is ignored.

sections.title: Shaft
sections.body: A drive wheel submits its RPS to the shaft with weight equal to its definition mass, 20, 25, 30, 40, 80, and the track mean spreads the shaft speed to every member. Slip against the ground still corrects each member's RPS before the mean.

Static analysis of one build. Tread speeds are the no-slip speed of the tyre surface; no vehicle speed, slip or force was measured in a running game.

For active, normally simulated vehicles, these formulas run once per nominal 1/60-second simulation update. Multiply per-update amounts by 60 for amounts per simulated second. A constant relaxation fraction k leaves (1-k)^60 of a gap after one simulated second. Physics solver substeps and render frames are separate; pauses, sleeping, unloaded vehicles and real-time slowdown are outside this conversion.

families.summary: Tread speed per RPS: Tank Wheel (Small) 2.513 m/s (9.048 km/h); Tank Wheel (Small/Wide) 2.513 m/s (9.048 km/h); Tank Wheel (Medium) 3.927 m/s (14.14 km/h); Tank Wheel (Large) 3.927 m/s (14.14 km/h); Tank Wheel (Huge) 6.283 m/s (22.62 km/h). Wheels in one track share one mean RPS.

sections.title: Speed per RPS
sections.body: Tank wheels use the road wheel's radius law at wheel_size 1: Tank Wheel (Small) 2.513 m/s (9.048 km/h); Tank Wheel (Small/Wide) 2.513 m/s (9.048 km/h); Tank Wheel (Medium) 3.927 m/s (14.14 km/h); Tank Wheel (Large) 3.927 m/s (14.14 km/h); Tank Wheel (Huge) 6.283 m/s (22.62 km/h). Medium and Large share radius 0.625 m, Small and Small/Wide 0.4 m.

sections.title: Tracks
sections.body: Tank wheels in one track share speed by a plain mean: the track pass adds each member's signed RPS, divides by the count and writes the mean back to every member. Two members at 10 and 0 RPS both leave at 5, whatever their radii, so tank wheels of different sizes in one track turn at one RPS but their treads move at different speeds. A tank wheel keeps its tyre factor 1 inside a track and halves it outside one, and keeps 0.975 of its RPS per update in a track and 0.7 outside one; the tyre type is ignored.

sections.title: Shaft
sections.body: Idler wheels have no RPS port. They take the track mean, which carries the drive wheels' shaft speed to them. Slip against the ground still corrects each member's RPS before the mean.

Static analysis of one build. Tread speeds are the no-slip speed of the tyre surface; no vehicle speed, slip or force was measured in a running game.

For active, normally simulated vehicles, these formulas run once per nominal 1/60-second simulation update. Multiply per-update amounts by 60 for amounts per simulated second. A constant relaxation fraction k leaves (1-k)^60 of a gap after one simulated second. Physics solver substeps and render frames are separate; pauses, sleeping, unloaded vehicles and real-time slowdown are outside this conversion.

families.summary: End rotor propellers with one power connection on the shared force-emitter law; at 10 RPS they give 10.755 or 21.489 and 13.633 or 27.289 internal force per RPS by air weight branch, the same as their through-drive counterparts.

sections.title: Thrust and shaft load
sections.body:
Each update the part reads its published shaft speed and computes w = RPS × 0.9999, the effective pitch p = clamp(saved pitch + input, -1, 1) and the load b = (2 × w × rotation_speed × π × blade_physics_length × p × 0.75 + p × U) × blade_efficiency × B × 0.32, where U is the relative flow along the thrust axis and B the number of intact blades. With q = clamp(b × 0.5 ÷ K, -10, 10), multiplied by 10 when the hub is below the water surface, it removes w × (1 - 1 ÷ (1 + q²)) RPS from its own speed and pushes with T = 1500 × K × removed RPS × efficiency, signed by the pitch.

The saved pitch starts at force_emitter_default_pitch 1, so effective pitch is clamp(1 + Collective): Collective -1 gives zero load and zero thrust, and 0 or more gives full pitch 1. Pitch alone cannot reverse their push; reversing the shaft does.

sections.title: Sizes
sections.body:
Rotor Propeller End (Small): K 120 or 60, 10.755 or 21.489 per RPS; Rotor Propeller End (Large): K 200 or 100, 13.633 or 27.289 per RPS. Figures are raw internal force per input RPS at 10 published RPS, effective pitch 1, 4 intact blades and no inflow, before the application cap.

Air parts take one of two solver weights, K = F ÷ 1000 or F × B ÷ 8000, depending on a definition byte the decode could not tie to a resource field; each figure gives both, the first for F ÷ 1000.

sections.title: End of a stack
sections.body: The end parts have no port B, so the binding installs no A/B link; they close a stack of through-drive parts. Because of the coaxial flag the rotor also applies two equal and opposite forces along local X, above and below the hub, each 800 × b × clamp(|saved pitch + Collective + 0.1|, 0, 1). They form a moment about the rotor axis that turns the vehicle against the rotor.

sections.title: Cyclic and hinge
sections.body:
Roll and Pitch, clamped to -1 to 1, move the point where the force acts by -4 × input along local X and Z and tilt the force direction by 0.4 × input. This tips the vehicle; no blade-by-blade phase is modelled.

The rotor body turns on a physical hinge whose motor is on while the RPS port is connected. Its impulse limit is 1000 for every size, and its target speed follows the speed the rotor kept on the previous update × force_emitter_rotation_speed.

sections.title: Water and altitude
sections.body:
With the hub below the water surface the rotor pushes not at all in this update, while its load ratio q is multiplied by 10, so it brakes the shaft much harder. The tooltip's decreased force is this cut-off.

Thrust is multiplied by (1 - 2.2413793e-5 × y)^5.3595023 of the vehicle's altitude y: 1 at sea level, 0 above 40000.

limitations: Internal force units before the 100 × S application cap. Open items shared by every propeller and rotor are listed under Propulsion.

For active, normally simulated vehicles, these formulas run once per nominal 1/60-second simulation update. Multiply per-update amounts by 60 for amounts per simulated second. A constant relaxation fraction k leaves (1-k)^60 of a gap after one simulated second. Physics solver substeps and render frames are separate; pauses, sleeping, unloaded vehicles and real-time slowdown are outside this conversion.

families.summary: Rotors with Power Connection A and B on the shared force-emitter law; the two ports are linked through the shaft solver with fraction 0.95 and ratio 1, and at 10 RPS the rotors give 26.603 or 52.979, 54.522 or 108.862 and 54.577 or 109.043 internal force per RPS by air weight branch.

sections.title: How the two ports share speed
sections.body: At binding the rotor links its A and B port nodes to each other. Every update the shaft solver adds each side's speed to the other side with weight × 0.95 at ratio 1, the same bridge a gearbox uses. The rotor's own load is submitted on A. There is no fixed split of power between the ports, and they do not take one speed at once: groups of weight 11 at 10 RPS on A and 21 at rest on B publish 3.55412 and 3.322734 RPS. Stacking rotors adds one link, and one more factor 0.95, per rotor.

sections.title: Thrust and shaft load
sections.body:
Each update the part reads its published shaft speed and computes w = RPS × 0.9999, the effective pitch p = clamp(saved pitch + input, -1, 1) and the load b = (2 × w × rotation_speed × π × blade_physics_length × p × 0.75 + p × U) × blade_efficiency × B × 0.32, where U is the relative flow along the thrust axis and B the number of intact blades. With q = clamp(b × 0.5 ÷ K, -10, 10), multiplied by 10 when the hub is below the water surface, it removes w × (1 - 1 ÷ (1 + q²)) RPS from its own speed and pushes with T = 1500 × K × removed RPS × efficiency, signed by the pitch.

The saved pitch starts at force_emitter_default_pitch 1, so effective pitch is clamp(1 + Collective): Collective -1 gives zero load and zero thrust, and 0 or more gives full pitch 1. Pitch alone cannot reverse their push; reversing the shaft does.

sections.title: Sizes
sections.body:
Rotor (Light): K 10 or 5, 26.603 or 52.979 per RPS; Rotor (Small): K 50 or 25, 54.522 or 108.862 per RPS; Rotor (Large): K 200 or 100, 54.577 or 109.043 per RPS. Figures are raw internal force per input RPS at 10 published RPS, effective pitch 1, 4 intact blades and no inflow, before the application cap.

Air parts take one of two solver weights, K = F ÷ 1000 or F × B ÷ 8000, depending on a definition byte the decode could not tie to a resource field; each figure gives both, the first for F ÷ 1000.

sections.title: Cyclic, hinge and reaction
sections.body:
Roll and Pitch, clamped to -1 to 1, move the point where the force acts by -4 × input along local X and Z and tilt the force direction by 0.4 × input. This tips the vehicle; no blade-by-blade phase is modelled.

The rotor body turns on a physical hinge whose motor is on while the RPS port is connected. Its impulse limit is 1000 for every size, and its target speed follows the speed the rotor kept on the previous update × force_emitter_rotation_speed.

Because of the coaxial flag the rotor also applies two equal and opposite forces along local X, above and below the hub, each 800 × b × clamp(|saved pitch + Collective + 0.1|, 0, 1). They form a moment about the rotor axis that turns the vehicle against the rotor.

sections.title: Water and altitude
sections.body:
With the hub below the water surface the rotor pushes not at all in this update, while its load ratio q is multiplied by 10, so it brakes the shaft much harder. The tooltip's decreased force is this cut-off.

Thrust is multiplied by (1 - 2.2413793e-5 × y)^5.3595023 of the vehicle's altitude y: 1 at sea level, 0 above 40000.

limitations: Internal force units before the 100 × S application cap. Open items shared by every propeller and rotor are listed under Propulsion.

For active, normally simulated vehicles, these formulas run once per nominal 1/60-second simulation update. Multiply per-update amounts by 60 for amounts per simulated second. A constant relaxation fraction k leaves (1-k)^60 of a gap after one simulated second. Physics solver substeps and render frames are separate; pauses, sleeping, unloaded vehicles and real-time slowdown are outside this conversion.

families.summary: Rotor propellers with Power Connection A and B on the shared force-emitter law; the ports are linked through the shaft solver with fraction 0.95 and ratio 1, and at 10 RPS they give 10.755 or 21.489 and 13.633 or 27.289 internal force per RPS by air weight branch.

sections.title: How the two ports share speed
sections.body: As on the through-drive rotors, the binding links ports A and B and the shaft solver mixes their speeds with weight × 0.95 at ratio 1. The load is submitted on A. Groups of weight 11 at 10 RPS and 21 at rest publish 3.55412 and 3.322734 RPS, so neither a fixed power share nor an instant common speed applies.

sections.title: Thrust and shaft load
sections.body:
Each update the part reads its published shaft speed and computes w = RPS × 0.9999, the effective pitch p = clamp(saved pitch + input, -1, 1) and the load b = (2 × w × rotation_speed × π × blade_physics_length × p × 0.75 + p × U) × blade_efficiency × B × 0.32, where U is the relative flow along the thrust axis and B the number of intact blades. With q = clamp(b × 0.5 ÷ K, -10, 10), multiplied by 10 when the hub is below the water surface, it removes w × (1 - 1 ÷ (1 + q²)) RPS from its own speed and pushes with T = 1500 × K × removed RPS × efficiency, signed by the pitch.

The saved pitch starts at force_emitter_default_pitch 1, so effective pitch is clamp(1 + Collective): Collective -1 gives zero load and zero thrust, and 0 or more gives full pitch 1. Pitch alone cannot reverse their push; reversing the shaft does.

sections.title: Sizes
sections.body:
Rotor Propeller (Small): K 120 or 60, 10.755 or 21.489 per RPS; Rotor Propeller (Large): K 200 or 100, 13.633 or 27.289 per RPS. Figures are raw internal force per input RPS at 10 published RPS, effective pitch 1, 4 intact blades and no inflow, before the application cap.

Air parts take one of two solver weights, K = F ÷ 1000 or F × B ÷ 8000, depending on a definition byte the decode could not tie to a resource field; each figure gives both, the first for F ÷ 1000.

sections.title: Cyclic, hinge and reaction
sections.body:
Roll and Pitch, clamped to -1 to 1, move the point where the force acts by -4 × input along local X and Z and tilt the force direction by 0.4 × input. This tips the vehicle; no blade-by-blade phase is modelled.

The rotor body turns on a physical hinge whose motor is on while the RPS port is connected. Its impulse limit is 1000 for every size, and its target speed follows the speed the rotor kept on the previous update × force_emitter_rotation_speed.

Because of the coaxial flag the rotor also applies two equal and opposite forces along local X, above and below the hub, each 800 × b × clamp(|saved pitch + Collective + 0.1|, 0, 1). They form a moment about the rotor axis that turns the vehicle against the rotor.

sections.title: Water and altitude
sections.body:
With the hub below the water surface the rotor pushes not at all in this update, while its load ratio q is multiplied by 10, so it brakes the shaft much harder. The tooltip's decreased force is this cut-off.

Thrust is multiplied by (1 - 2.2413793e-5 × y)^5.3595023 of the vehicle's altitude y: 1 at sea level, 0 above 40000.

findings.label: Through-drive coupling example
findings.detail: Group A (I = 11, 10 RPS) and group B (I = 21, at rest) joined by one through-drive link (h = 0.95, ratio 1): A publishes (11 × 10 + 0) ÷ (11 + 21 × 0.95) = 3.55412 RPS and B (0 + 10 × 11 × 0.95) ÷ (21 + 11 × 0.95) = 3.322734 RPS on the same update. families.summary: Each extension cuts the battle cannon's spread multiplier by 0.2, to no less than 0.5, without changing muzzle speed or the recoil coefficient.

sections.title: Accuracy
sections.body: Each accepted extension of the battle cannon's class subtracts 0.2 from its spread multiplier m, down to 0.5. The battle cannon's spread goes from ±0.0025 rad per axis to ±0.002, ±0.0015 and ±0.00125 with one, two and three or more extensions.

sections.title: What it does not change
sections.body: Muzzle speed comes from the gun's class record and the firing body only, so an extension does not make rounds faster. It moves the muzzle forward by 0.25 × 3 = 0.75 per part and adds its mass to the vehicle; the recoil coefficient and multiplier stay as they are.

findings.detail: The dispersion is multiplied by the spread multiplier m at component+0x37c (0x14042892c) and by 0.25, giving the half-width. families.summary: Each extension cuts the heavy autocannon's spread multiplier by 0.2, to no less than 0.5, without changing muzzle speed or the recoil coefficient.

sections.title: Accuracy
sections.body: Each accepted extension of the heavy autocannon's class subtracts 0.2 from its spread multiplier m, down to 0.5. The heavy autocannon's spread goes from ±0.0025 rad per axis to ±0.002, ±0.0015 and ±0.00125 with one, two and three or more extensions.

sections.title: What it does not change
sections.body: Muzzle speed comes from the gun's class record and the firing body only, so an extension does not make rounds faster. It moves the muzzle forward by 0.25 × 3 = 0.75 per part and adds its mass to the vehicle; the recoil coefficient and multiplier stay as they are.

sections.title: Tooltip wording
sections.body: gun_m_barrel's tooltip says extensions add weight; gun_m_barrel_1 to gun_m_barrel_3 say they produce more recoil force, as the light autocannon extension does. All four are weapon_type 4 with weapon_class 3, and the walk has no branch on tooltip text, so they share one accuracy rule. None raises the recoil coefficient; the extra mass of 20 per part changes how the vehicle responds.

sections.title: Accuracy
sections.body: Each accepted extension of the rotary autocannon's class subtracts 0.2 from its spread multiplier m, down to 0.5. The rotary autocannon's spread goes from ±0.005 rad per axis to ±0.004, ±0.003 and ±0.0025 with one, two and three or more extensions.

sections.title: What it does not change
sections.body: Muzzle speed comes from the gun's class record and the firing body only, so an extension does not make rounds faster. It moves the muzzle forward by 0.25 × 4 = 1 per part and adds its mass to the vehicle; the recoil coefficient and multiplier stay as they are.

families.summary: Each extension cuts the bertha cannon's spread multiplier by 0.2, to no less than 0.5, without changing muzzle speed or the recoil coefficient.

sections.title: Accuracy
sections.body: Each accepted extension of the bertha cannon's class subtracts 0.2 from its spread multiplier m, down to 0.5. The bertha cannon's spread goes from ±0.00125 rad per axis to ±0.001, ±0.00075 and ±0.000625 with one, two and three or more extensions.

sections.title: What it does not change
sections.body: Muzzle speed comes from the gun's class record and the firing body only, so an extension does not make rounds faster. It moves the muzzle forward by 0.25 × 4 = 1 per part and adds its mass to the vehicle; the recoil coefficient and multiplier stay as they are.

sections.title: Speed per RPS
sections.body: r = wheel_radius - 0.125 + 0.125 × wheel_size metres and the tyre surface moves at 2π × r × RPS m/s: Wheel 3x3 2.199 m/s (7.917 km/h); Wheel 5x5 3.644 m/s (13.12 km/h); Wheel 7x7 5.341 m/s (19.23 km/h); Wheel 9x9 6.597 m/s (23.75 km/h). Each 0.1 of wheel_size adds 0.0125 m to r. Under drive or braking the wheel slips, so the vehicle's speed differs from the tread speed.

sections.title: Grip and shaft
sections.body: Slip relative to the ground, capped at 5 m/s, asks for grip in proportion to grip_factor × tyre factor ÷ r; the default tyre type 1 has factor 0.1875 and double wheels start at 1.75 instead of 1. Contact also pulls the wheel's RPS toward the ground speed (inference). The wheel submits that RPS to its shaft with weight 10, 20, 40, 80 (its definition mass), so grip loads the engine. Brake multiplies the RPS by 1 - brake each update.

sections.title: Suspension
sections.body: The definitions carry flag 0x800000. The update then sets the ray spring's stiffness and damping to 0, so it adds no chassis force, and moves its offsets to L = 0.3 × r and a = 0.8 × r. The second request, 60 × tyre_pressure × (max(0, 0.2 × r + 0.8 × r - l) + 4 × (l_old - l)), and the wheel's sphere body remain. The flag changes neither the tread speed nor the grip.

findings.label: Component updates per simulated second

Static analysis of one build. Tread speeds are the no-slip speed of the tyre surface; no vehicle speed, slip or force was measured in a running game.

For active, normally simulated vehicles, these formulas run once per nominal 1/60-second simulation update. Multiply per-update amounts by 60 for amounts per simulated second. A constant relaxation fraction k leaves (1-k)^60 of a gap after one simulated second. Physics solver substeps and render frames are separate; pauses, sleeping, unloaded vehicles and real-time slowdown are outside this conversion.

families.summary: Tread speed per RPS at wheel_size 1: Wheel 3x3 (Suspension) 2.199 m/s (7.917 km/h); Wheel 5x5 (Suspension) 3.644 m/s (13.12 km/h); Wheel 7x7 (Suspension) 5.341 m/s (19.23 km/h); Wheel 9x9 (Suspension) 6.597 m/s (23.75 km/h).

sections.title: Speed per RPS
sections.body: r = wheel_radius - 0.125 + 0.125 × wheel_size metres and the tyre surface moves at 2π × r × RPS m/s: Wheel 3x3 (Suspension) 2.199 m/s (7.917 km/h); Wheel 5x5 (Suspension) 3.644 m/s (13.12 km/h); Wheel 7x7 (Suspension) 5.341 m/s (19.23 km/h); Wheel 9x9 (Suspension) 6.597 m/s (23.75 km/h). Each 0.1 of wheel_size adds 0.0125 m to r. Under drive or braking the wheel slips, so the vehicle's speed differs from the tread speed.

sections.title: Grip and shaft
sections.body: Slip relative to the ground, capped at 5 m/s, asks for grip in proportion to grip_factor × tyre factor ÷ r; the default tyre type 1 has factor 0.1875 and double wheels start at 1.75 instead of 1. Contact also pulls the wheel's RPS toward the ground speed (inference). The wheel submits that RPS to its shaft with weight 10.5, 21, 42, 84 (0.7 × its definition mass), so grip loads the engine. Brake multiplies the RPS by 1 - brake each update.

sections.title: Suspension
sections.body: The chassis spring pushes with 60 × tyre_pressure × (k × max(0, 1.5 × r - l) + c × (l_old - l)), l being the ray distance, k = 0.05 + 0.45 × stiffness_factor and c = 0.5 + 4.5 × damping_factor. The defaults 0.4 and 0.11 give k = 0.23 and c = 0.995. Raise stiffness_factor for less sag and damping_factor for less bounce (inference); tyre_pressure scales both.

Static analysis of one build. Tread speeds are the no-slip speed of the tyre surface; no vehicle speed, slip or force was measured in a running game.

For active, normally simulated vehicles, these formulas run once per nominal 1/60-second simulation update. Multiply per-update amounts by 60 for amounts per simulated second. A constant relaxation fraction k leaves (1-k)^60 of a gap after one simulated second. Physics solver substeps and render frames are separate; pauses, sleeping, unloaded vehicles and real-time slowdown are outside this conversion.

families.summary: rudder_surface_area 8, 20, 40, 70 and 120 across the five wing sizes. The air force scales linearly with it, and the wing term lifts even at zero angle of attack.

sections.title: Variant tradeoffs
sections.body: At the same body mass, airspeed, altitude and angle, the computed wing force scales linearly with rudder_surface_area: 8, 20, 40, 70 and 120, or 1, 2.5, 5, 8.75 and 15 times the small wing. The application cap can limit the gain on a light craft. The listed voxel count is not a multiplier.

sections.title: Wing lift
sections.body: Wing sections have rudder_type 1. On top of the normal airspeed they get a wing term 3 × c^5 × g, where c is the cosine between the direction of travel and the wing's forward axis (the reverse of dynamic_rotation_axes) and g rises from 0 at 15 m/s to 1 at 40 m/s. That term gives lift with the wing level in the airflow. Travelling backwards along that axis removes it. Wings have no Rotation input, so their angle to the airflow comes from how they are mounted and how the craft flies.

sections.title: Example
sections.body: A small wing section (area 8) on a body of mass 1000 at sea level, 30 m/s and 10° angle of attack gets a normal force of 594.2 internal units: 585.1 lift and 103.2 drag. The XXL wing makes 15 times that under the same conditions.
